The **Smithsonian Institution** ([/s m ɪ θ ˈ s oʊ n i ə n/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_smith-SOH-nee-ən_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); or simply the **Smithsonian**) is a group of [museums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum "Museum"), [education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_center "Education center") and [research centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_institute "Research institute"), created by the [United States federal government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States") "for the increase and diffusion of knowledge".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-:3-4) Founded on August 10, 1846, it operates as a trust instrumentality[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-5) and is not formally a part of any of the [three branches of the federal government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States#branches "Federal government of the United States").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-6) The institution is named after its founding donor, British scientist [James Smithson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Smithson "James Smithson").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-about_SI-7) It was originally organized as the **United States National Museum**, but that name ceased to exist administratively in 1967.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-8)

The Smithsonian Institution has historical holdings of over 157 million items,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-9) 21 museums, 21 libraries, 14 education and research centers, a zoo, and historical and architectural landmarks, mostly located in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-about_SI-7)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-10)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-:3-4) Additional facilities are located in [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), and [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia"). More than 200 institutions and museums in 47 [states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._states "U.S. states"),[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-11)[Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico"), and [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama") are [Smithsonian Affiliates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Affiliations "Smithsonian Affiliations").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-13) Institution publications include _[Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian\_(magazine) "Smithsonian (magazine)")_ and _[Air & Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air\_&\_Space "Air & Space")_ magazines.

Almost all of the institution's 30 million annual visitors[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-14) are admitted without charge,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-:3-4) the exception being visitors to [Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Hewitt,_Smithsonian_Design_Museum "Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum") in New York City, which charges an admissions fee.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-15) The Smithsonian's annual budget is around $1.25 billion, with two-thirds coming from annual federal appropriations.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-16) Other funding comes from the institution's [endowment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_endowment "Financial endowment"), private and corporate contributions, membership dues, and earned retail, concession, and licensing revenue.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-about_SI-7) As of 2024, the institution's endowment had a total value of about $2.6 billion.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-17)

## Founding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Founding")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Washington%2C_D.C.%2C_April_1865_34773v.jpg/250px-Washington%2C_D.C.%2C_April_1865_34773v.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Washington,_D.C.,_April_1865_34773v.jpg)

"[The Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution_Building "Smithsonian Institution Building")" (built 1847) in April 1865.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Smithsonian_Building_NR.jpg/250px-Smithsonian_Building_NR.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Smithsonian_Building_NR.jpg)

"The Castle" on the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall"): the institution's earliest building remains its headquarters.

In many ways, the origin of the Smithsonian Institution can be traced to a group of Washington citizens who, being "impressed with the importance of forming an association for promoting useful knowledge," met on June 28, 1816, to establish the [Columbian Institute for the Promotion of Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_Institute_for_the_Promotion_of_Arts_and_Sciences "Columbian Institute for the Promotion of Arts and Sciences").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-18) Officers were elected in October 1816, and the organization was granted a charter by Congress on April 20, 1818 (this charter expired in 1838). [Benjamin Latrobe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Latrobe "Benjamin Latrobe"), who was architect for the US Capitol after the War of 1812, and [William Thornton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Thornton "William Thornton"), the architect who designed [the Octagon House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Octagon_House "The Octagon House") and [Tudor Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudor_Place "Tudor Place"), served as officers. Other prominent members, who numbered from 30 to 70 during the institute's existence, included [John Quincy Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams "John Quincy Adams"), [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson"), [Henry Clay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Clay "Henry Clay"), Judge [William Cranch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Cranch "William Cranch"), and [James Hoban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hoban "James Hoban"). Honorary members included [James Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison "James Madison"), [James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe "James Monroe"), [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams"), [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson"), and the [Marquis de Lafayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquis_de_Lafayette "Marquis de Lafayette"). Operating expenses were covered from the $5 yearly dues collected from each member.

The institute proposed a number of undertakings. These included the study of plant life and the creation of a botanical garden on the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall"), an examination of the country's mineral production, improvement in the management and care of livestock, and the writing of a topographical and statistical history of the United States. Reports were to be published periodically to share this knowledge with the greater public, but due to a lack of funds, this initially did not occur. The institute first met in Blodget's Hotel, later in the Treasury Department and City Hall, before being assigned a permanent home in 1824 in the Capitol building.

Beginning in 1825, weekly sittings were arranged during sessions of Congress for the reading of scientific and literary productions, but this was done for only a short time, as the number of attendees declined rapidly. Eighty-five communications by 26 people were made to Congress during the entire life of the society, with more than a half relating to astronomy or mathematics. Among all the activities planned by the institute, only a few were actually implemented. Two were the establishment of a botanical garden, and a museum that was designed to have a national and permanent status. The former occupied space where the present [Botanic Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Botanic_Garden "United States Botanic Garden") sits.

The museum contained specimens of zoology, botany, archeology, fossils, etc., some of which were passed on to the Smithsonian Institution after its formation. The institute's charter expired in 1838, but its spirit lived on in the [National Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_for_the_Promotion_of_Science "National Institute for the Promotion of Science"), founded in 1840. With the mission to "promote science and the useful arts, and to establish a national museum of natural history," this organization continued to press Congress to establish a museum that would be structured in terms that were very similar to those finally incorporated into the founding of the Smithsonian Institution. Its work helped to develop an underlying philosophy that pushed for the pursuit and development of scientific knowledge that would benefit the nation, and edify its citizens at the same time.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-19)

The British scientist [James Smithson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Smithson "James Smithson") (1765–1829) left most of his wealth to his nephew Henry James Hungerford. When Hungerford died childless in 1835,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-nephewdead-20)[_[new archival link needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Archiving\_a\_source "Help:Archiving a source")_] the estate passed "to the United States of America, to found at Washington, under the name of the Smithsonian institution, an establishment for the increase & diffusion of Knowledge among men", in accordance with Smithson's [will](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:James_Smithson_photocopied_will_3_of_3.jpg "wikisource:Page:James Smithson photocopied will 3 of 3.jpg").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-will-21) Congress officially accepted the legacy bequeathed to the nation and pledged the faith of the United States to the charitable trust on July 1, 1836.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-foundingfactsheet-22) The American diplomat [Richard Rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Rush "Richard Rush") was dispatched to England by President [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson") to collect the bequest. Rush returned in August 1838 with 105 sacks containing 104,960 [gold sovereigns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_sovereign "Gold sovereign"). This was approximately $500,000 at the time; when considering the GDP at the time, it may have been equivalent to about $220 million in the year 2007.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-gardens-24)

Once the money was in hand, eight years of congressional haggling ensued over how to interpret Smithson's rather vague mandate "for the increase and diffusion of knowledge."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-foundingfactsheet-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-gardens-24) The money was invested by the US Treasury in bonds issued by the state of Arkansas, which soon defaulted. After heated debate, Massachusetts representative (and former president) [John Quincy Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams "John Quincy Adams") persuaded Congress to restore the lost funds with interest[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-25) and, despite designs on the money for other purposes, convinced his colleagues to preserve it for an institution of science and learning.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-26) Finally, on August 10, 1846, President [James K. Polk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Polk "James K. Polk") signed the legislation that established the Smithsonian Institution as a trust instrumentality of the United States, to be administered by a [Board of Regents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Regents "Board of Regents") and a secretary of the Smithsonian.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-foundingfactsheet-22)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-27)

## Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Development")]

Though the Smithsonian's first secretary, [Joseph Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Henry "Joseph Henry"), wanted the institution to be a center for scientific research,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-28) it also became the depository for various Washington and U.S. government collections.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-29) The [United States Exploring Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Exploring_Expedition "United States Exploring Expedition") by the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") circumnavigated the globe between 1838 and 1842.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-University_of_Washington_Press-30) The voyage amassed thousands of animal specimens, an [herbarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbarium "Herbarium") of 50,000 plant specimens, and diverse shells and minerals, tropical birds, jars of seawater, and [ethnographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnographic "Ethnographic") artifacts from the [South Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Pacific_Ocean "South Pacific Ocean").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-University_of_Washington_Press-30) These specimens and artifacts became part of the Smithsonian collections,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-31) as did those collected by several military and civilian surveys of the [American West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_United_States "Western United States"), including the [Mexican Boundary Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_and_Mexican_Boundary_Survey "United States and Mexican Boundary Survey") and [Pacific Railroad Surveys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Railroad_Surveys "Pacific Railroad Surveys"), which assembled many [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") artifacts and [natural history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_history "Natural history") specimens.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-32)

In 1846, the regents developed a plan for weather observation; in 1847, money was appropriated for meteorological research.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-33) The institution became a magnet for young [scientists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientists "Scientists") from 1857 to 1866, who formed a group called the [Megatherium Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megatherium_Club "Megatherium Club").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-Merrill1999-34) The Smithsonian played a critical role as the US partner institution in early bilateral scientific exchanges with the [Academy of Sciences of Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_Cuba "Academy of Sciences of Cuba").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-35)

### Museums and buildings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Museums and buildings")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Smithsonian.jpg/330px-Smithsonian.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Smithsonian.jpg)

The Smithsonian Institution area around the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall").

Construction began on the [Smithsonian Institution Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution_Building "Smithsonian Institution Building") ("the Castle") in 1849. Designed by architect [James Renwick Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Renwick_Jr. "James Renwick Jr."), its interiors were completed by general contractor Gilbert Cameron. The building opened in 1855.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-36)

The Smithsonian's first expansion came with the construction of the [Arts and Industries Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_and_Industries_Building "Arts and Industries Building") in 1881. Congress had promised to build a new structure for the museum if the 1876 [Philadelphia Centennial Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Centennial_Exposition "Philadelphia Centennial Exposition") generated enough income. It did, and the building was designed by architects [Adolf Cluss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Cluss "Adolf Cluss") and Paul Schulze, based on original plans developed by [Major General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_general_(United_States) "Major general (United States)")[Montgomery C. Meigs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_C._Meigs "Montgomery C. Meigs") of the [United States Army Corps of Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Corps_of_Engineers "United States Army Corps of Engineers"). It opened in 1881.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-37)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/A_field_trip_to_the_Smithsonian_Institution_LCCN2001702329.jpg/250px-A_field_trip_to_the_Smithsonian_Institution_LCCN2001702329.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_field_trip_to_the_Smithsonian_Institution_LCCN2001702329.jpg)

A school field trip to the Smithsonian Institution, c.1899

The [National Zoological Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Zoological_Park_(United_States) "National Zoological Park (United States)") opened in 1889 to accommodate the Smithsonian's Department of Living Animals.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-siarchives.si.edu-38) The park was designed by landscape architect [Frederick Law Olmsted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Law_Olmsted "Frederick Law Olmsted").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-siarchives.si.edu-38)

The [National Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Natural_History "National Museum of Natural History") opened in June 1911 to similarly accommodate the Smithsonian's United States National Museum, which had previously been housed in the Castle and then the Arts and Industries Building.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-39) This structure was designed by the D.C. architectural firm of [Hornblower & Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hornblower_&_Marshall "Hornblower & Marshall").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-40)

When [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit")[philanthropist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philanthropist "Philanthropist")[Charles Lang Freer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lang_Freer "Charles Lang Freer") donated his private collection to the Smithsonian and funds to build the museum to hold it (which was named the [Freer Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freer_Gallery "Freer Gallery")), it was among the Smithsonian's first major donations from a private individual.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-41) The gallery opened in 1923.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-42)

More than 40 years would pass before the next museum, the Museum of History and Technology (renamed the [National Museum of American History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History "National Museum of American History") in 1980), opened in 1964. It was designed by the world-renowned firm of [McKim, Mead & White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKim,_Mead_&_White "McKim, Mead & White").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-43) The [Anacostia Community Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anacostia_Community_Museum "Anacostia Community Museum"), an "experimental store-front" museum created at the initiative of Smithsonian Secretary [S. Dillon Ripley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S._Dillon_Ripley "S. Dillon Ripley"), opened in the [Anacostia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anacostia "Anacostia") neighborhood of Washington, D.C., in 1967.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-Bass-44)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-SIAHistory-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-Oehser-46) That same year, the Smithsonian signed an agreement to take over the Cooper Union Museum for the Arts of Decoration (now the [Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Hewitt,_Smithsonian_Design_Museum "Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum")).[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-47) The [National Portrait Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Portrait_Gallery_(United_States) "National Portrait Gallery (United States)") and the [Smithsonian American Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_American_Art_Museum "Smithsonian American Art Museum") opened in the [Old Patent Office Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Patent_Office_Building "Old Patent Office Building") (built in 1867) on October 7, 1968.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-49) The reuse of an older building continued with the opening of the [Renwick Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renwick_Gallery "Renwick Gallery") in 1972 in the 1874 Renwick-designed art gallery originally built by local philanthropist [William Wilson Corcoran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wilson_Corcoran "William Wilson Corcoran") to house the [Corcoran Gallery of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corcoran_Gallery_of_Art "Corcoran Gallery of Art").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-WP_2013-50)

The first new museum building to open since the National Museum of History and Technology was the [Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirshhorn_Museum_and_Sculpture_Garden "Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden"), which opened in 1974.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-51) The [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum"), the Smithsonian's largest in terms of floor space, opened July 1, 1976.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-52)

Eleven years later, the [National Museum of African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_Art "National Museum of African Art") and the [Arthur M. Sackler Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_M._Sackler_Gallery "Arthur M. Sackler Gallery") opened in a new, joint, underground museum between the Freer Gallery and the Smithsonian Castle.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-SIAA-53)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-opening-54)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-SIA1-55) Reuse of another old building came in 1993 with the opening of the [National Postal Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Postal_Museum "National Postal Museum") in the 1904 former [City Post Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_Square_Building "Postal Square Building") building, a few city blocks from the Mall.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-56)

In 2004, the Smithsonian opened the [National Museum of the American Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_the_American_Indian "National Museum of the American Indian") in a new building near the [United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol "United States Capitol").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-57) Twelve years later almost to the day, in 2016, the latest museum opened: the [National Museum of African American History and Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_American_History_and_Culture "National Museum of African American History and Culture"), in a new building near the [Washington Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Monument "Washington Monument").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-58)

Two more museums have been established and are being planned for eventual construction on the Mall: the [National Museum of the American Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_the_American_Latino "National Museum of the American Latino") and the [Smithsonian American Women's History Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_American_Women's_History_Museum "Smithsonian American Women's History Museum").

### Capital campaigns

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Capital campaigns")]

In 2011, the Smithsonian undertook its first-ever capital fundraising campaign.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-59) The $1.5 billion effort raised $1 billion at the three-year mark. Smithsonian officials made the campaign public in October 2014 in an effort to raise the remaining $500 million. More than 60,000 individuals and organizations donated money to the campaign by the time it went public.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-McGlone-60) This included 192 gifts of at least $1 million.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-McGlone-60) Members of the boards of directors of various Smithsonian museums donated $372 million.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-McGlone-60) The Smithsonian said that funds raised would go toward completion of the [National Museum of African American History and Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_American_History_and_Culture "National Museum of African American History and Culture") building, and renovations of the [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum"), [National Museum of American History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History "National Museum of American History"), and the [Renwick Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renwick_Gallery "Renwick Gallery").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-McGlone-60) A smaller amount of funds would go to educational initiatives and digitization of collections.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-McGlone-60) As of September 2017, the Smithsonian claimed to have raised $1.79 billion, with three months left in the formal campaign calendar.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-61)

Separately from the major capital campaign, the Smithsonian has begun fundraising through [Kickstarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kickstarter "Kickstarter").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-62) An example is a campaign to fund the preservation and maintenance of the [ruby slippers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby_slippers "Ruby slippers") worn by [Judy Garland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judy_Garland "Judy Garland") for her role as [Dorothy Gale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Gale "Dorothy Gale") in the 1939 film _[The Wizard of Oz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wizard\_of\_Oz\_(1939\_film) "The Wizard of Oz (1939 film)")_.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-63)

### Collections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Collections")]

Smithsonian collections total more than 155 million artworks, artifacts, and specimens, the largest such holdings of any museum complex in the world.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-91)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-si-facts-92) The [National Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Natural_History "National Museum of Natural History") accounts for more than 148 million of these, mostly scientific specimens, the single largest component being its invertebrate zoology collection of over 49.8 million specimens.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-nmnh-facts-93)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-si-collections-fs-94) About half of the Natural History collection is stored at the Smithsonian's Museum Support Center in [Suitland, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suitland,_Maryland "Suitland, Maryland").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-nmnh-facts-93) The Smithsonian Institution Libraries hold roughly 2.1 million volumes, and the Smithsonian Archives hold about 162,000 cubic feet (4,600 m 3) of archival material.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-si-collections-fs-94) Only a small fraction of the collections—estimated at less than one percent—is on public display at any given time, with the remainder maintained for research; the Collections Search Center makes 9.9 million digital records available online.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-95)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-si-collections-fs-94)

The Smithsonian Institution has many categories of displays that can be visited at the museums. In 1912, First Lady [Helen Herron Taft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Herron_Taft "Helen Herron Taft") donated her inauguration gown to the museum to begin the [First Ladies' Gown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_gown#First_Ladies_Collection "Ball gown") display at the National Museum of American History,[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-96) one of the Smithsonian's most popular exhibits.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-97) The museum displays treasures such as the [Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star-Spangled_Banner_(flag) "Star-Spangled Banner (flag)"), the stove pipe hat that was worn by President [Abraham Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln "Abraham Lincoln"), the ruby slippers worn by Judy Garland in _[The Wizard Of Oz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wizard\_of\_Oz\_(1939\_film) "The Wizard of Oz (1939 film)")_, and the original Teddy Bear that was named after President [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-98) In 2016, the Smithsonian's Air & Space museum curators restored the large model _Enterprise_ from the original _[Star Trek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Trek:\_The\_Original\_Series "Star Trek: The Original Series")_ TV series.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-99)

#### Ethical returns and repatriation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Ethical returns and repatriation")]

Following international debates about the [decolonisation of museums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation_of_museums "Decolonisation of museums") and the legal and moral justifications of their acquisitions, the Smithsonian adopted a new "ethical returns policy" on April 29, 2022. This will permit the [deaccession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deaccessioning "Deaccessioning") and restitution of items collected under circumstances considered unethical by contemporary standards and thus places moral over legal arguments. A month before, the Smithsonian's [National Museum of African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_Art "National Museum of African Art") had announced the planned return of most of its 39 [Benin Bronzes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benin_Bronzes "Benin Bronzes") to [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria"),[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-100) as well as of other cultural items to [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-101)

On October 11, 2022, Benin Bronzes from the National Museum of African Art, as well as the [National Gallery of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery_of_Art "National Gallery of Art"), were formally returned to Nigerian cultural officials in a ceremony held in Washington, D.C. The Nigerian Minister of Information and Culture, [Lai Mohammed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lai_Mohammed "Lai Mohammed"), and Prince Aghatise Erediauwa, representing the [Oba of Benin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oba_of_Benin "Oba of Benin") Kingdom, spoke at the ceremony. Mohammed said the "decision to return the timeless artworks is worth emulating."[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-102)

The Smithsonian also faced scrutiny over its holdings of human remains. The institution holds the remains of more than 30,000 individuals, mostly at the National Museum of Natural History and including roughly 250 brains, largely acquired in the 19th and early 20th centuries without consent.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-wexler-103) After a 2023 _[Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ investigation into a collection of brains amassed largely from marginalized residents, the Smithsonian formed a Human Remains Task Force in April 2023.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-104) In February 2024 the task force recommended that the institution not collect, display, or use human remains for research without the consent of the deceased or their descendants, and that it work toward returning all remains regardless of cultural affiliation.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-wexler-103) Under the [National Museum of the American Indian Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_the_American_Indian_Act "National Museum of the American Indian Act") of 1989, the Smithsonian had already repatriated or made available for return the remains of more than 7,500 individuals.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-105)

### Open access

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Open access")]

On February 25, 2020, the Smithsonian launched Smithsonian Open Access, releasing about 2.8 million two- and three-dimensional images and roughly 173 years of staff-created data into the public domain under a [Creative Commons Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Commons_license#CC0 "Creative Commons license") (CC0) dedication, allowing anyone to download, reuse, and modify the material without permission or charge.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-106)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-solly-107) At the time it was described as the largest and most interdisciplinary open-access release by a museum, drawing on material from all of the Smithsonian's museums, research centers, libraries, archives, and the National Zoo.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-solly-107) The collection has continued to grow to more than five million images.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-108)

## Cultural centers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Cultural centers")]

The Smithsonian Institution includes three cultural centers among its units:

*   [Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Folklife_and_Cultural_Heritage "Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage")
*   [Smithsonian Asian Pacific American Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Asian_Pacific_American_Center "Smithsonian Asian Pacific American Center")
*   [Smithsonian Latino Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Latino_Center "Smithsonian Latino Center")

### Smithsonian Latino Center

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Smithsonian Latino Center")]

In 1997, the Smithsonian Latino Center was created as a way to recognize Latinos across the Smithsonian Institution. The primary purpose of the center is to place Latino contributions to the arts, history, science, and national culture across the Smithsonian's museums and research centers.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-:0-125)

The center is a division of the Smithsonian Institution.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-:1-126) As of May 2016, the center is run by an executive director, Eduardo Díaz.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-127)

#### History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: History")]

At the time of its creation, the Smithsonian Institution had other entities dedicated to other minority groups: National Museum of the American Indian, Freer-Sackler Gallery for Asian Arts and Culture, African Art Museum, and the National Museum of African-American Heritage and Culture.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-:2-128)

The opening of the center was prompted, in part, by the publishing of a report called "Willful Neglect: The Smithsonian and U.S. Latinos".[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-:2-128)

According to documents obtained by _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_, when former Latino Center executive director [Pilar O'Leary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilar_O'Leary "Pilar O'Leary") first took the job, the center faced employees who had "serious performance issues". No performance plans existed for the staff and unfulfilled financial obligations to sponsors existed. The website's quality was poor, and the center did not have a public affairs manager, a programs director, adequate human resources support, or cohesive mission statement.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-:2-128)

After difficult times in the first few years, the center improved. According to the Smithsonian, the center "support[s] scholarly research, exhibitions, public and educational programs, web-based content and virtual platforms, and collections and archives. [It] also manage[s] leadership and professional development programs for Latino youth, emerging scholars and museum professionals."[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-:0-125) Today, the website features a high-tech virtual museum including self-guided virtual tours of past and present exhibits.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-129)

#### Young Ambassadors Program

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Young Ambassadors Program")]

The Smithsonian Latino Center's Young Ambassadors Program (YAP) is a program within the Latino Center that reaches out to Latino high school students with the goal of encouraging them to become leaders in arts, sciences, and the humanities.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-130)

Students selected for the program travel to Washington, D.C. for an "enrichment seminar" that lasts approximately five days. Afterwards, students return to their communities to serve in a paid, one-month internship.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-:1-126)

Pilar O'Leary launched the program when she served as executive director of the Smithsonian Latino Center.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-131) According to the Latino Center, O'Leary told the press in 2007: "Our goal is to help our Young Ambassadors become the next generation of leaders in the arts and culture fields. This program encourages students to be proud of their roots and learn more about their cultural heritage to inspire them to educate the public in their own communities about how Latinos are enriching America's cultural fabric."[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-:1-126)

## Publications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section:  Publications")]

The institution publishes _[Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian\_(magazine) "Smithsonian (magazine)")_ magazine monthly and _Air & Space Quarterly_. _Smithsonian_ was the result of Secretary of the Smithsonian [S. Dillon Ripley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S._Dillon_Ripley "S. Dillon Ripley") asking the retired editor of _[Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life\_(magazine) "Life (magazine)")_ magazine [Edward K. Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_K._Thompson "Edward K. Thompson") to produce a magazine "about things in which the Smithsonian Institution is interested, might be interested or ought to be interested".[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-132) Another Secretary of the Smithsonian, Walter Boyne, founded _Air & Space_.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-133)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-134)_[Air & Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air\_&\_Space "Air & Space")_ magazine was published bimonthly from 1986 to 2022.

The organization publishes under the imprints Smithsonian Institution Press, Smithsonian Books, and Smithsonian Institution Scholarly Press.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-open-lib-sip-135)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-smithsonian-books-136)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-scholarly-press-137)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Awards")]

The Smithsonian makes a number of awards to acknowledge and support meritorious work.

*   The [James Smithson Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Smithson_Medal "James Smithson Medal"), the Smithsonian Institution's highest award, was established in 1965 and is given in recognition of exceptional contributions to art, science, history, education, and technology.
*   The James Smithson Bicentennial Medal, established in 1965, is given to persons who have made distinguished contributions to the advancement of areas of interest to the Smithsonian.
*   The [Hodgkins Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodgkins_Medal "Hodgkins Medal"), established in 1893, is awarded for important contributions to the understanding of the physical environment.
*   The Henry Medal, established in 1878, is presented to individuals in recognition of their distinguished service, achievements or contributions to the prestige and growth of the Smithsonian Institution.
*   The [Langley Gold Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langley_Gold_Medal "Langley Gold Medal") is awarded for meritorious investigations in connection with aerodromics ("the science or art of [flying aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft "Aircraft")", a 19th-century term predating the [powered airplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airplane "Airplane"))[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-138) and its application to aviation.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-139)

## Administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Administration")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Smithsonian_Castle_Doorway.jpg/250px-Smithsonian_Castle_Doorway.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Smithsonian_Castle_Doorway.jpg)

The Smithsonian Castle doorway

The Smithsonian Institution was established as a [trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trust_(property) "Trust (property)") instrumentality by act of Congress.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-Stam-140) More than two-thirds of the Smithsonian's workforce of some 6,300 persons are employees of the federal government. The [Smithsonian Institution Office of Protection Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution_Office_of_Protection_Services "Smithsonian Institution Office of Protection Services") oversees security at the Smithsonian facilities and enforces laws and regulations for [National Capital Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Capital_Parks "National Capital Parks") together with the [United States Park Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Park_Police "United States Park Police").

The president's 2011 budget proposed just under $800 million in support for the Smithsonian, slightly increased from previous years. Institution exhibits are free of charge, though in 2010 the [Deficit Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Commission_on_Fiscal_Responsibility_and_Reform "National Commission on Fiscal Responsibility and Reform") recommended admission fees.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-141)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-142)

As approved by [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") on August 10, 1846, the legislation that created the Smithsonian Institution called for the creation of a Board of Regents to govern and administer the organization.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-Stam-140) This seventeen-member board meets at least four times a year and includes as _[ex officio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex\_officio "Ex officio")_ members the [chief justice of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_United_States "Chief Justice of the United States") and the [vice president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States"). The nominal head of the institution is the [chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education) "Chancellor (education)"), an office which has traditionally been held by the chief justice. In September 2007, the board created the position of chair of the Board of Regents, a position currently held by [Risa Lavizzo-Mourey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risa_Lavizzo-Mourey "Risa Lavizzo-Mourey").[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-143)

Other members of the Board of Regents are three members of the [U.S. House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives") appointed by the [speaker of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the United States House of Representatives"); three members of the Senate, appointed by the [president _pro tempore_ of the Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_the_United_States#Officers "Senate of the United States"); and nine citizen members, nominated by the board and approved by the Congress in a joint resolution signed by the president of the United States.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-144) Regents who are senators or representatives serve for the duration of their elected terms, while citizen Regents serve a maximum of two 6-year terms. Regents are compensated on a part-time basis.

The [chief executive officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer") (CEO) of the Smithsonian is the secretary, who is appointed by the Board of Regents. The secretary also serves as secretary to the Board of Regents but is not a voting member of that body. The secretary of the Smithsonian has the [privilege of the floor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_Rules_of_the_United_States_Senate,_Rule_XXIII "Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXIII") at the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The fourteenth and current secretary is [Lonnie Bunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonnie_Bunch "Lonnie Bunch"), who was appointed in 2019 after serving as the founding director of the Smithsonian's [National Museum of African American History and Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_American_History_and_Culture "National Museum of African American History and Culture").[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-NPR1-145) On September 8, 2026, Bunch announced that he would retire as secretary.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-146)

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Controversies")]

### _Enola Gay_ display

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Enola Gay display")]

See also: [_Enola Gay_ exhibition controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enola_Gay#Exhibition_controversy "Enola Gay")

In 1995, controversy arose over the exhibit at the [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum") with the display of the _[Enola Gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enola\_Gay "Enola Gay")_, the [Superfortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superfortress "Superfortress") used by the United States to drop the first [atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb") used in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). The [American Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Legion "American Legion") and [Air Force Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Association "Air Force Association") believed the exhibit put forward only one side of the [debate over the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debate_over_the_atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki "Debate over the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki"), and that it emphasized the effect on victims without discussing its use within the overall context of the war.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-180) The Smithsonian changed the exhibit, displaying the aircraft only with associated technical data and without discussion of its historic role in the war.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-181)

### Censorship of _Seasons of Life and Land_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Censorship of Seasons of Life and Land")]

In 2003, a [National Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Natural_History "National Museum of Natural History") exhibit, [Subhankar Banerjee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subhankar_Banerjee_(photographer) "Subhankar Banerjee (photographer)")'s _Seasons of Life and Land_, featuring photographs of the [Arctic National Wildlife Refuge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_National_Wildlife_Refuge "Arctic National Wildlife Refuge"), was censored and moved to the basement by Smithsonian officials. They were concerned that its subject matter was too politically controversial.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-182)

In November 2007, _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ reported internal criticism has been raised regarding the institution's handling of the exhibit on the Arctic. According to documents and e-mails, the exhibit and its associated presentation were edited at high levels to add "scientific uncertainty" regarding the nature and impact of [global warming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming "Global warming") on the [Arctic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic "Arctic"). Acting Secretary of the Smithsonian [Cristián Samper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cristi%C3%A1n_Samper "Cristián Samper") was interviewed by the _Post_, and claimed the exhibit was edited because it contained conclusions that went beyond what could be proven by contemporary [climatology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climatology "Climatology").[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-183) The Smithsonian is now a participant in the [U.S. Global Change Research Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Global_Change_Research_Program "U.S. Global Change Research Program").[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-184)

### Copyright restrictions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Smithsonian_Institution&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Copyright restrictions")]

The Smithsonian Institution provides access to its image collections for educational, scholarly, and nonprofit uses. Commercial uses are generally restricted unless permission is obtained. Smithsonian images fall into different copyright categories; some are protected by copyright, many are subject to license agreements or other contractual conditions, and some fall into the public domain, such as those prepared by Smithsonian employees as part of their official duties. The Smithsonian's terms of use for its digital content, including images, are set forth on the Smithsonian Web site.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-185)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-186)

In April 2006, the institution entered into an agreement of "first refusal" rights for its vast [silent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") and [public domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain "Public domain") film archives with [Showtime Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Showtime_Networks "Showtime Networks"), mainly for use on the [Smithsonian Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Channel "Smithsonian Channel"), a network created from this deal. Critics contend this agreement effectively gives Showtime control over the film archives, as it requires filmmakers to obtain permission from the network to use extensive amounts of film footage from the Smithsonian archives.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Museum#cite_note-187)
