The **Colorado State Capitol Building**, located at 200 East Colfax Avenue in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"), Colorado, United States, is the home of the [Colorado General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_General_Assembly "Colorado General Assembly") and the offices of the [Governor of Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Colorado "Governor of Colorado"), [Lieutenant Governor of Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Governor_of_Colorado "Lieutenant Governor of Colorado"), and the [Colorado State Treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Treasurer "Colorado State Treasurer").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Colorado_State_Capitol&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The building is intentionally reminiscent of the [United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol "United States Capitol"). Designed by [Elijah E. Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elijah_E._Myers "Elijah E. Myers"), it was constructed in the 1890s from Colorado white granite, and opened for use in November 1894. The General Assembly first convened inside the building on January 2, 1895.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-2) The distinctive gold dome consists of real [gold leaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_leaf "Gold leaf"), first added in 1908, commemorating the [Colorado Gold Rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Gold_Rush "Colorado Gold Rush"). The building is part of Denver's [Civic Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic_Center,_Denver "Civic Center, Denver") area. It was listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") as part of the Civic Center Historic District in 1974,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-nom-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-nrhpdoc-NPS-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-nrhpdoc-NARA-5) and became part of the Denver Civic Center [National Historic Landmark District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark_District "National Historic Landmark District") in 2012.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-weekly-6)

A major safety upgrade project, funded by the Colorado State Historical Fund, was started in 2001 and completed in 2009.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-7) The design by [Fentress Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fentress_Architects "Fentress Architects") added modern safety features, like enclosed stair towers, that blended in with the original architecture.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-8) The Colorado Capitol Building is featured on many of Denver's architectural tours.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-LetsRoam-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-Rocky_Mountain_Tours-10)

## Building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Colorado_State_Capitol&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Building")]

Serving as the beginning of the Capitol Hill district, the historic building sits slightly higher than the rest of downtown Denver. The main entrance hall is open 180 feet (55 m) to the top of the dome, about the height of an 18-story building. Additionally, the official elevation of Denver is measured outside the west entrance to the building, where the fifteenth step is engraved with the words "One Mile Above Sea Level". From this step, at 5,280 feet (1,609 m), the sun can be seen setting behind the [Rocky Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains "Rocky Mountains"). A second mile high marker was set in the 18th step in 1969 when [Colorado State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_University "Colorado State University") students resurveyed the elevation. In 2003, a more accurate measurement was made with modern means, and the 13th step was identified as being one mile (1.6 km) high, where a 3rd marker was installed.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-11)

### Materials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Colorado_State_Capitol&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Materials")]

The [superstructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superstructure "Superstructure") of the building was constructed using [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite") from the [Aberdeen Quarry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeen_Quarry "Aberdeen Quarry") near [Gunnison, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunnison,_Colorado "Gunnison, Colorado"). Approximately 280,000 cubic feet (7,900 m 3) or 24,000 tons of the granite were quarried for the building. This gray granite forms the exterior of the building. The interior of the building uses a large amount of Colorado Rose Onyx, a rare rose [marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble "Marble") from a quarry near [Beulah, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beulah_Valley,_Colorado "Beulah Valley, Colorado"). The amount used in the building consumed the entire known supply. White [Yule Marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yule_Marble "Yule Marble") from the quarries near [Marble, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble,_Colorado "Marble, Colorado") was also used throughout the capitol for the floors. Many designs have been found in the marble including an image resembling [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") and another of [Molly Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Brown "Molly Brown").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-Everett-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-Colorado-13)

Many of the windows are made of [stained glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass "Stained glass"), depicting people or events related to the [history of Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Colorado "History of Colorado"). The halls are decorated with portraits of every [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States"), with all the presidents from [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") to [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") being painted by Lawrence Williams. Painter Sarah A. Boardman took over from Williams, and has since painted [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") and the [original portrait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol_portrait_of_Donald_Trump "Colorado State Capitol portrait of Donald Trump") of [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), which was removed after Trump criticized it and replaced with one by Arizonan artist Vanessa Horabuena.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-14) Colorado artist Kirsten Savage painted President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")'s portrait.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-15) One of the contractors for the construction of the Colorado State Capitol building was Illinois building contractor William Douglas Richardson, who was the president of the W. D. Richardson Construction Company.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-colorado-16) Richardson had participated in numerous major building contracts throughout the United States, and was interconnected with the [Jacob Bunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Bunn "Jacob Bunn") and [John Whitfield Bunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Whitfield_Bunn "John Whitfield Bunn") network of corporations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-17)

The **Colorado State Capitol Building**, located at 200 East Colfax Avenue in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"), Colorado, United States, is the home of the [Colorado General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_General_Assembly "Colorado General Assembly") and the offices of the [Governor of Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Colorado "Governor of Colorado"), [Lieutenant Governor of Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Governor_of_Colorado "Lieutenant Governor of Colorado"), and the [Colorado State Treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Treasurer "Colorado State Treasurer").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Colorado_State_Capitol&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The building is intentionally reminiscent of the [United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol "United States Capitol"). Designed by [Elijah E. Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elijah_E._Myers "Elijah E. Myers"), it was constructed in the 1890s from Colorado white granite, and opened for use in November 1894. The General Assembly first convened inside the building on January 2, 1895.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-2) The distinctive gold dome consists of real [gold leaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_leaf "Gold leaf"), first added in 1908, commemorating the [Colorado Gold Rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Gold_Rush "Colorado Gold Rush"). The building is part of Denver's [Civic Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic_Center,_Denver "Civic Center, Denver") area. It was listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") as part of the Civic Center Historic District in 1974,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-nom-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-nrhpdoc-NPS-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-nrhpdoc-NARA-5) and became part of the Denver Civic Center [National Historic Landmark District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark_District "National Historic Landmark District") in 2012.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-weekly-6)

A major safety upgrade project, funded by the Colorado State Historical Fund, was started in 2001 and completed in 2009.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-7) The design by [Fentress Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fentress_Architects "Fentress Architects") added modern safety features, like enclosed stair towers, that blended in with the original architecture.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-8) The Colorado Capitol Building is featured on many of Denver's architectural tours.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-LetsRoam-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-Rocky_Mountain_Tours-10)

## Building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Colorado_State_Capitol&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Building")]

Serving as the beginning of the Capitol Hill district, the historic building sits slightly higher than the rest of downtown Denver. The main entrance hall is open 180 feet (55 m) to the top of the dome, about the height of an 18-story building. Additionally, the official elevation of Denver is measured outside the west entrance to the building, where the fifteenth step is engraved with the words "One Mile Above Sea Level". From this step, at 5,280 feet (1,609 m), the sun can be seen setting behind the [Rocky Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains "Rocky Mountains"). A second mile high marker was set in the 18th step in 1969 when [Colorado State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_University "Colorado State University") students resurveyed the elevation. In 2003, a more accurate measurement was made with modern means, and the 13th step was identified as being one mile (1.6 km) high, where a 3rd marker was installed.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-11)

### Materials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Colorado_State_Capitol&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Materials")]

The [superstructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superstructure "Superstructure") of the building was constructed using [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite") from the [Aberdeen Quarry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeen_Quarry "Aberdeen Quarry") near [Gunnison, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunnison,_Colorado "Gunnison, Colorado"). Approximately 280,000 cubic feet (7,900 m 3) or 24,000 tons of the granite were quarried for the building. This gray granite forms the exterior of the building. The interior of the building uses a large amount of Colorado Rose Onyx, a rare rose [marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble "Marble") from a quarry near [Beulah, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beulah_Valley,_Colorado "Beulah Valley, Colorado"). The amount used in the building consumed the entire known supply. White [Yule Marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yule_Marble "Yule Marble") from the quarries near [Marble, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble,_Colorado "Marble, Colorado") was also used throughout the capitol for the floors. Many designs have been found in the marble including an image resembling [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") and another of [Molly Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Brown "Molly Brown").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-Everett-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-Colorado-13)

Many of the windows are made of [stained glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass "Stained glass"), depicting people or events related to the [history of Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Colorado "History of Colorado"). The halls are decorated with portraits of every [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States"), with all the presidents from [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") to [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") being painted by Lawrence Williams. Painter Sarah A. Boardman took over from Williams, and has since painted [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") and the [original portrait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol_portrait_of_Donald_Trump "Colorado State Capitol portrait of Donald Trump") of [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), which was removed after Trump criticized it and replaced with one by Arizonan artist Vanessa Horabuena.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-14) Colorado artist Kirsten Savage painted President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")'s portrait.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-15) One of the contractors for the construction of the Colorado State Capitol building was Illinois building contractor William Douglas Richardson, who was the president of the W. D. Richardson Construction Company.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-colorado-16) Richardson had participated in numerous major building contracts throughout the United States, and was interconnected with the [Jacob Bunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Bunn "Jacob Bunn") and [John Whitfield Bunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Whitfield_Bunn "John Whitfield Bunn") network of corporations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_Capitol#cite_note-17)

The **Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture** (commonly as **Burke Museum**) is the [natural history museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_history_museum "Natural history museum") of the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") in [Seattle, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"). It is administered by the [Arts Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_College_of_Arts_and_Sciences#Arts_Division "University of Washington College of Arts and Sciences") of the [College of Arts and Sciences of the University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_College_of_Arts_and_Sciences "University of Washington College of Arts and Sciences").

Established in 1899 as the **Washington State Museum**, the museum traces its origins to a high school naturalist club formed in 1879. The museum is the oldest in Washington state and boasts a collection of more than 16 million artifacts, including the world's largest collection of spread bird wings. The Burke Museum is the official state museum of Washington.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Young Naturalists Society

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Young Naturalists Society")]

The roots of the Burke Museum can be traced to a natural history club formed by high school students in the 19th century. The group was formed in December 1879 by students [Edmond S. Meany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_S._Meany "Edmond S. Meany"), J. O. Young, P. Brooks Randolph, and Charles Denny. Denny's father, city founder [Arthur Denny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_A._Denny "Arthur A. Denny"), was a regent of the [Territorial University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") and arranged for the group to meet on campus. The Young Naturalists adopted a constitution and bylaws, and the official name "Young Naturalists Society", in 1880. As the founding members graduated high school and matriculated to the university, the membership of the Young Naturalists expanded to include university students.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/YoungNaturalistsClubhouse.jpg/250px-YoungNaturalistsClubhouse.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:YoungNaturalistsClubhouse.jpg)

The Young Naturalists Society clubhouse in Seattle, pictured probably in the late 1800s.

In 1882 Orson "Bug" Johnson (Orson Bennett Johnson[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-5)) was retained as a biology instructor at the University of Washington, bringing 20,000 animal specimens with him. Johnson immediately involved himself with the Young Naturalists, and the addition of his collection gave the club the largest natural history collection in the [Pacific Northwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Northwest "Pacific Northwest"). Under Johnson's direction, the Young Naturalists began expanding this nucleus of specimens and artifacts, which were stored in a backroom of the Denny home.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-6) A permanent structure to house the growing collection was built on the Territorial University's campus in 1886, with the club soliciting donations to fund its construction. Many specimens in the collection were regularly borrowed by university faculty to assist in instruction.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-uww-7)

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/17/Orson_Bennett_Johnson.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Orson_Bennett_Johnson.png)

Orson "Bug" Johnson led the Young Naturalists to acquire the largest natural history collection in the Pacific Northwest.

In the 1890s Edmond Meany returned to teach history at the university. He led a revitalization of the group that he had helped found a decade before, bringing in new members, including women. By this point the society's collection had grown to include more than 60,000 specimens.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-8)

### Transition to the Washington State Museum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Transition to the Washington State Museum")]

The University of Washington moved its campus from downtown Seattle to its present location in 1895. The portion of the Young Naturalists collection that had been used in university instruction was relocated to the university's Denny Hall while the remainder stayed in the Young Naturalists clubhouse downtown. In 1899 the [Washington State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Legislature "Washington State Legislature") designated the portion of Denny Hall used to house the collection as the Washington State Museum.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-9) In 1904 the Young Naturalists voted to donate the rest of their collection to the Washington State Museum and disband.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

### Carousel of buildings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Carousel of buildings")]

The 1909 [Alaska–Yukon–Pacific Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska%E2%80%93Yukon%E2%80%93Pacific_Exposition "Alaska–Yukon–Pacific Exposition") (AYP Expo) brought a boon of construction to the University of Washington's campus. When the fair ended, the Washington State Museum moved into its first dedicated building, the fair's former California Building.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Washington_State_Museum%2C_University_of_Washington_campus%2C_Seattle%2C_1922_%28COBB_344%29.jpeg/250px-Washington_State_Museum%2C_University_of_Washington_campus%2C_Seattle%2C_1922_%28COBB_344%29.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Washington_State_Museum,_University_of_Washington_campus,_Seattle,_1922_(COBB_344).jpeg)

Washington State Museum in the former Forestry Building in 1922. The building was constructed for the AYPE Exposition

Persistent leaks in that facility caused it to later relocate to the fair's former Forestry Building which, it was soon discovered, was infested with bark beetles. For four years, from 1923 to 1927, the museum's collections were disbursed around campus.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

The situation was finally resolved in 1927 when the museum moved into what had originally been constructed as the Washington State Building for the AYP Expo.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-10)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Washington_State_Building.jpg/250px-Washington_State_Building.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Washington_State_Building.jpg)

This photograph of the Washington State Building, later the Washington State Museum, was taken probably in 1909.

In 1929, Erna Gunther became the museum's director, a post she would hold for more than 25 years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

The museum found itself, once again, displaced in 1957 after its AYP Expo-era building was condemned.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

### New name and buildings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: New name and buildings")]

When [Thomas Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Burke_(Seattle) "Thomas Burke (Seattle)") died in 1925, his wife, [Caroline McGilvra Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_McGilvra_Burke?action=edit&redlink=1 "Caroline McGilvra Burke (page does not exist)"), sought an appropriate monument for her husband that would "advance the cause of a better mutual understanding between ... the people of the Pacific shores." A collector of [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") artifacts herself, she bequeathed her personal collection to the museum following her death in 1932. The Burke estate offered to help fund a new state museum, with one major stipulation - the structure had to be named after Burke. Some University officials balked at this, as did Erna Gunther. The institution had been known as the Washington State Museum since 1899, and the Burke funds would only go toward a third of the construction costs. Other funds came from a [National Science Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation "National Science Foundation") grant, but the new building was still smaller than one that Erna Gunther recommended. Nevertheless, the new facility was ultimately dedicated on May 3, 1964, with its new director, [Walter Fairservis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Fairservis "Walter Fairservis"), at the helm.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Burke_Museum_new_building_under_construction%2C_2018.jpg/250px-Burke_Museum_new_building_under_construction%2C_2018.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burke_Museum_new_building_under_construction,_2018.jpg)

The new building under construction in early 2018

In 1996, the museum launched a ten-year plan to move its exhibition space off campus and into a downtown Seattle location. Under the proposal, curators and preservationists would continue to work at the University of Washington while exhibits would be hosted at a new site. The proposal ultimately did not materialize. In 2014, the museum made another push for a new facility, asking the [Washington State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Legislature "Washington State Legislature") for half the $95 million needed to construct a 110,000 square-foot facility to replace its current building.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-11) The new Burke Museum building finished construction in 2018, and the old building closed at the end of the year to transfer the collection's 16 million items before its demolition in April 2019.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-Times-Move-12) The new museum cost $106 million to construct and opened to the public on October 12, 2019.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-reopening-ref-13) The new building, designed by UW alum [Tom Kundig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Kundig "Tom Kundig"), features large windows into research areas to showcase parts of the collection that were not previously exhibited. A garden with 60 species of Washington-native plants has been planted around the new building and its adjacent courtyard, designed to host small events.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-14) The new museum also has a small cafe, Off the Rez, that serves [Native American cuisine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_cuisine "Native American cuisine").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-15)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Burke_Museum_Main_Entrance_-_21_January_2020.jpg/250px-Burke_Museum_Main_Entrance_-_21_January_2020.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burke_Museum_Main_Entrance_-_21_January_2020.jpg)

Main entrance to the new Burke Museum building in January 2020.

## Collections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Collections")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Burke_Museum_totem_poles_01.jpg/250px-Burke_Museum_totem_poles_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burke_Museum_totem_poles_01.jpg)

Totem poles outside the Burke Museum

The museum houses more than 16 million artifacts and specimens in its anthropology, biology, and geology research divisions. According to the museum, its ornithology division includes the largest collection of spread bird wings in the world, while the museum's collection of frozen bird tissues is the world's second largest. The [Mammalogy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammalogy "Mammalogy") Collection, which is managed by University of Washington professor and Burke Museum curator [Sharlene Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharlene_Santana "Sharlene Santana"), contains more than 55,000 mammal specimens, and is regarded as the 10th largest collection of mammals in a North American university.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-16) The museum states that its collection of [Northwest Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Northwest "Pacific Northwest")[ethnographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnography "Ethnography") material is the fifth largest collection of Native American art in the world, numbering 10,000 objects, among which are "the important early Swan, Eells, Emmons, and Waters collections, as well as the unmatched Blackman-Hall and Ottenberg contemporary [silkscreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silkscreen "Silkscreen")[print](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_master_print "Old master print") collections, and the Steinman contemporary Northwest Coast sculpture collection."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-washington1-17) The museum's Northwest Coast image research database includes "the Holm/Wright collection of images of Northwest Coast art from 200 museums and private collections, the Harris collection of Northwest Coast silver jewelry images, and de Menil photographs of Northwest Coast [totem poles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totem_pole "Totem pole"), as well as the George MacDonald Archive of historical Northwest Coast photographs."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-washington1-17)

## Exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Exhibits")]

### Past long-term exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Past long-term exhibits")]

Prior to its temporary closure in 2018, the museum displayed three long-term exhibits: "Life and Times of Washington State", "Pacific Voices", and "Treasures of the Burke". "Life and Times of Washington State" was a natural history exhibit on the 545-million-year evolution of the Northwest region. Features of this exhibit included large-scale fossils such as an _[Allosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allosaurus "Allosaurus")_ skeleton cast and a [giant ground sloth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_ground_sloth "Giant ground sloth") fossil found during the construction of [Sea-Tac International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle-Tacoma_International_Airport "Seattle-Tacoma International Airport"). There were also displays that explained the geologic history of the area and its influence on the terrain and climate.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-18)

"Pacific Voices" was a cultural exhibit that told the stories or traditions of 19 different [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") and [Pacific Rim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Rim "Pacific Rim") cultures through art, artifacts, ceremonial objects, and audio/visual documentaries.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-19)

### Temporary exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Temporary exhibits")]

The Burke also hosts a schedule of different exhibits throughout the year in its temporary gallery. These changing exhibits include traveling exhibits organized by other institutions and original exhibits curated by Burke staff. In November 2022 the Burke hosted "Body Language: Reawakening Cultural Tattooing of the Northwest."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-20)

### Present long-term exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Present long-term exhibits")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Baird%27s_beaked_whale_skeleton_Burke_Museum_Seattle.jpg/250px-Baird%27s_beaked_whale_skeleton_Burke_Museum_Seattle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baird's_beaked_whale_skeleton_Burke_Museum_Seattle.jpg)

A skeleton of a [Baird’s beaked whale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baird's_beaked_whale "Baird's beaked whale") is displayed in the main lobby. This specimen washed ashore on a Washington beach in 2015.

The museum reopened in its new building on October 12, 2019, with several new exhibits:[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-reopening-ref-13) "Culture is Living", "Northwest Native Art", "Amazing Life", "Our Material World", and "Fossils Uncovered". Each gallery focuses on a particular category of Washington State natural history and culture.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-21) In "Culture is Living", patrons can engage with objects past and present and hear from community across the Pacific.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-22) "Fossils Uncovered" includes one of the best-preserved _T. rex_ skulls in the world, as well as numerous other fossils.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-23)

## Museum governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Museum governance")]

### Governing body

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Governing body")]

The museum is administered through the [University of Washington College of Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_College_of_Arts_and_Sciences "University of Washington College of Arts and Sciences");[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-26) the [University of Washington Board of Regents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_Board_of_Regents "University of Washington Board of Regents") serves as the museum's governing body.

### BMA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: BMA")]

The Burke Museum Association (BMA) is an organization made up of the Burke's board of trustees and an advisory council. Their mission is to actively support the Burke Museum by increasing public visibility, raising public and private funds to support programming and future expansion, and providing strong ties to the community.

### Funding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Funding")]

In 2009, the museum had an annual budget of about $5 million, half of which came from an appropriation from the state of Washington. The budget did not include substantial in-kind support provided by the University of Washington as owner of the Burke property. Other sources of funding include interest from its endowment (10 percent), foundation grants and individual donations (27 percent), and admission fees and gift shop sales (13 percent).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-rep-2)

The **Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture** (commonly as **Burke Museum**) is the [natural history museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_history_museum "Natural history museum") of the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") in [Seattle, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"). It is administered by the [Arts Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_College_of_Arts_and_Sciences#Arts_Division "University of Washington College of Arts and Sciences") of the [College of Arts and Sciences of the University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_College_of_Arts_and_Sciences "University of Washington College of Arts and Sciences").

Established in 1899 as the **Washington State Museum**, the museum traces its origins to a high school naturalist club formed in 1879. The museum is the oldest in Washington state and boasts a collection of more than 16 million artifacts, including the world's largest collection of spread bird wings. The Burke Museum is the official state museum of Washington.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Young Naturalists Society

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Young Naturalists Society")]

The roots of the Burke Museum can be traced to a natural history club formed by high school students in the 19th century. The group was formed in December 1879 by students [Edmond S. Meany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_S._Meany "Edmond S. Meany"), J. O. Young, P. Brooks Randolph, and Charles Denny. Denny's father, city founder [Arthur Denny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_A._Denny "Arthur A. Denny"), was a regent of the [Territorial University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") and arranged for the group to meet on campus. The Young Naturalists adopted a constitution and bylaws, and the official name "Young Naturalists Society", in 1880. As the founding members graduated high school and matriculated to the university, the membership of the Young Naturalists expanded to include university students.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/YoungNaturalistsClubhouse.jpg/250px-YoungNaturalistsClubhouse.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:YoungNaturalistsClubhouse.jpg)

The Young Naturalists Society clubhouse in Seattle, pictured probably in the late 1800s.

In 1882 Orson "Bug" Johnson (Orson Bennett Johnson[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-5)) was retained as a biology instructor at the University of Washington, bringing 20,000 animal specimens with him. Johnson immediately involved himself with the Young Naturalists, and the addition of his collection gave the club the largest natural history collection in the [Pacific Northwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Northwest "Pacific Northwest"). Under Johnson's direction, the Young Naturalists began expanding this nucleus of specimens and artifacts, which were stored in a backroom of the Denny home.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-6) A permanent structure to house the growing collection was built on the Territorial University's campus in 1886, with the club soliciting donations to fund its construction. Many specimens in the collection were regularly borrowed by university faculty to assist in instruction.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-uww-7)

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/17/Orson_Bennett_Johnson.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Orson_Bennett_Johnson.png)

Orson "Bug" Johnson led the Young Naturalists to acquire the largest natural history collection in the Pacific Northwest.

In the 1890s Edmond Meany returned to teach history at the university. He led a revitalization of the group that he had helped found a decade before, bringing in new members, including women. By this point the society's collection had grown to include more than 60,000 specimens.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-8)

### Transition to the Washington State Museum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Transition to the Washington State Museum")]

The University of Washington moved its campus from downtown Seattle to its present location in 1895. The portion of the Young Naturalists collection that had been used in university instruction was relocated to the university's Denny Hall while the remainder stayed in the Young Naturalists clubhouse downtown. In 1899 the [Washington State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Legislature "Washington State Legislature") designated the portion of Denny Hall used to house the collection as the Washington State Museum.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-9) In 1904 the Young Naturalists voted to donate the rest of their collection to the Washington State Museum and disband.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

### Carousel of buildings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Carousel of buildings")]

The 1909 [Alaska–Yukon–Pacific Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska%E2%80%93Yukon%E2%80%93Pacific_Exposition "Alaska–Yukon–Pacific Exposition") (AYP Expo) brought a boon of construction to the University of Washington's campus. When the fair ended, the Washington State Museum moved into its first dedicated building, the fair's former California Building.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Washington_State_Museum%2C_University_of_Washington_campus%2C_Seattle%2C_1922_%28COBB_344%29.jpeg/250px-Washington_State_Museum%2C_University_of_Washington_campus%2C_Seattle%2C_1922_%28COBB_344%29.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Washington_State_Museum,_University_of_Washington_campus,_Seattle,_1922_(COBB_344).jpeg)

Washington State Museum in the former Forestry Building in 1922. The building was constructed for the AYPE Exposition

Persistent leaks in that facility caused it to later relocate to the fair's former Forestry Building which, it was soon discovered, was infested with bark beetles. For four years, from 1923 to 1927, the museum's collections were disbursed around campus.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

The situation was finally resolved in 1927 when the museum moved into what had originally been constructed as the Washington State Building for the AYP Expo.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-10)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Washington_State_Building.jpg/250px-Washington_State_Building.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Washington_State_Building.jpg)

This photograph of the Washington State Building, later the Washington State Museum, was taken probably in 1909.

In 1929, Erna Gunther became the museum's director, a post she would hold for more than 25 years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

The museum found itself, once again, displaced in 1957 after its AYP Expo-era building was condemned.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

### New name and buildings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: New name and buildings")]

When [Thomas Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Burke_(Seattle) "Thomas Burke (Seattle)") died in 1925, his wife, [Caroline McGilvra Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_McGilvra_Burke?action=edit&redlink=1 "Caroline McGilvra Burke (page does not exist)"), sought an appropriate monument for her husband that would "advance the cause of a better mutual understanding between ... the people of the Pacific shores." A collector of [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") artifacts herself, she bequeathed her personal collection to the museum following her death in 1932. The Burke estate offered to help fund a new state museum, with one major stipulation - the structure had to be named after Burke. Some University officials balked at this, as did Erna Gunther. The institution had been known as the Washington State Museum since 1899, and the Burke funds would only go toward a third of the construction costs. Other funds came from a [National Science Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation "National Science Foundation") grant, but the new building was still smaller than one that Erna Gunther recommended. Nevertheless, the new facility was ultimately dedicated on May 3, 1964, with its new director, [Walter Fairservis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Fairservis "Walter Fairservis"), at the helm.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-his-4)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Burke_Museum_new_building_under_construction%2C_2018.jpg/250px-Burke_Museum_new_building_under_construction%2C_2018.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burke_Museum_new_building_under_construction,_2018.jpg)

The new building under construction in early 2018

In 1996, the museum launched a ten-year plan to move its exhibition space off campus and into a downtown Seattle location. Under the proposal, curators and preservationists would continue to work at the University of Washington while exhibits would be hosted at a new site. The proposal ultimately did not materialize. In 2014, the museum made another push for a new facility, asking the [Washington State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Legislature "Washington State Legislature") for half the $95 million needed to construct a 110,000 square-foot facility to replace its current building.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-11) The new Burke Museum building finished construction in 2018, and the old building closed at the end of the year to transfer the collection's 16 million items before its demolition in April 2019.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-Times-Move-12) The new museum cost $106 million to construct and opened to the public on October 12, 2019.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-reopening-ref-13) The new building, designed by UW alum [Tom Kundig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Kundig "Tom Kundig"), features large windows into research areas to showcase parts of the collection that were not previously exhibited. A garden with 60 species of Washington-native plants has been planted around the new building and its adjacent courtyard, designed to host small events.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-14) The new museum also has a small cafe, Off the Rez, that serves [Native American cuisine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_cuisine "Native American cuisine").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-15)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Burke_Museum_Main_Entrance_-_21_January_2020.jpg/250px-Burke_Museum_Main_Entrance_-_21_January_2020.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burke_Museum_Main_Entrance_-_21_January_2020.jpg)

Main entrance to the new Burke Museum building in January 2020.

## Collections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Collections")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Burke_Museum_totem_poles_01.jpg/250px-Burke_Museum_totem_poles_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burke_Museum_totem_poles_01.jpg)

Totem poles outside the Burke Museum

The museum houses more than 16 million artifacts and specimens in its anthropology, biology, and geology research divisions. According to the museum, its ornithology division includes the largest collection of spread bird wings in the world, while the museum's collection of frozen bird tissues is the world's second largest. The [Mammalogy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammalogy "Mammalogy") Collection, which is managed by University of Washington professor and Burke Museum curator [Sharlene Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharlene_Santana "Sharlene Santana"), contains more than 55,000 mammal specimens, and is regarded as the 10th largest collection of mammals in a North American university.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-16) The museum states that its collection of [Northwest Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Northwest "Pacific Northwest")[ethnographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnography "Ethnography") material is the fifth largest collection of Native American art in the world, numbering 10,000 objects, among which are "the important early Swan, Eells, Emmons, and Waters collections, as well as the unmatched Blackman-Hall and Ottenberg contemporary [silkscreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silkscreen "Silkscreen")[print](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_master_print "Old master print") collections, and the Steinman contemporary Northwest Coast sculpture collection."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-washington1-17) The museum's Northwest Coast image research database includes "the Holm/Wright collection of images of Northwest Coast art from 200 museums and private collections, the Harris collection of Northwest Coast silver jewelry images, and de Menil photographs of Northwest Coast [totem poles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totem_pole "Totem pole"), as well as the George MacDonald Archive of historical Northwest Coast photographs."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-washington1-17)

## Exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Exhibits")]

### Past long-term exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Past long-term exhibits")]

Prior to its temporary closure in 2018, the museum displayed three long-term exhibits: "Life and Times of Washington State", "Pacific Voices", and "Treasures of the Burke". "Life and Times of Washington State" was a natural history exhibit on the 545-million-year evolution of the Northwest region. Features of this exhibit included large-scale fossils such as an _[Allosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allosaurus "Allosaurus")_ skeleton cast and a [giant ground sloth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_ground_sloth "Giant ground sloth") fossil found during the construction of [Sea-Tac International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle-Tacoma_International_Airport "Seattle-Tacoma International Airport"). There were also displays that explained the geologic history of the area and its influence on the terrain and climate.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-18)

"Pacific Voices" was a cultural exhibit that told the stories or traditions of 19 different [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") and [Pacific Rim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Rim "Pacific Rim") cultures through art, artifacts, ceremonial objects, and audio/visual documentaries.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-19)

### Temporary exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Temporary exhibits")]

The Burke also hosts a schedule of different exhibits throughout the year in its temporary gallery. These changing exhibits include traveling exhibits organized by other institutions and original exhibits curated by Burke staff. In November 2022 the Burke hosted "Body Language: Reawakening Cultural Tattooing of the Northwest."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-20)

### Present long-term exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Present long-term exhibits")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Baird%27s_beaked_whale_skeleton_Burke_Museum_Seattle.jpg/250px-Baird%27s_beaked_whale_skeleton_Burke_Museum_Seattle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baird's_beaked_whale_skeleton_Burke_Museum_Seattle.jpg)

A skeleton of a [Baird’s beaked whale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baird's_beaked_whale "Baird's beaked whale") is displayed in the main lobby. This specimen washed ashore on a Washington beach in 2015.

The museum reopened in its new building on October 12, 2019, with several new exhibits:[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-reopening-ref-13) "Culture is Living", "Northwest Native Art", "Amazing Life", "Our Material World", and "Fossils Uncovered". Each gallery focuses on a particular category of Washington State natural history and culture.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-21) In "Culture is Living", patrons can engage with objects past and present and hear from community across the Pacific.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-22) "Fossils Uncovered" includes one of the best-preserved _T. rex_ skulls in the world, as well as numerous other fossils.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-23)

## Museum governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Museum governance")]

### Governing body

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Governing body")]

The museum is administered through the [University of Washington College of Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_College_of_Arts_and_Sciences "University of Washington College of Arts and Sciences");[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-26) the [University of Washington Board of Regents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_Board_of_Regents "University of Washington Board of Regents") serves as the museum's governing body.

### BMA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: BMA")]

The Burke Museum Association (BMA) is an organization made up of the Burke's board of trustees and an advisory council. Their mission is to actively support the Burke Museum by increasing public visibility, raising public and private funds to support programming and future expansion, and providing strong ties to the community.

### Funding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Funding")]

In 2009, the museum had an annual budget of about $5 million, half of which came from an appropriation from the state of Washington. The budget did not include substantial in-kind support provided by the University of Washington as owner of the Burke property. Other sources of funding include interest from its endowment (10 percent), foundation grants and individual donations (27 percent), and admission fees and gift shop sales (13 percent).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture#cite_note-rep-2)

The **National Museum of Natural History** (**NMNH**) is a [natural history museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_history_museum "Natural history museum") administered by the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution"), located on the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall") in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), United States. It has free admission and is open 364 days a year. It received 3.3 million visits in 2025.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-4)

Opened in 1910, the museum on the National Mall was one of the first Smithsonian buildings constructed exclusively to hold the national collections and research facilities.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-RC-5) The main building has an overall area of 1.5 million square feet (140,000 m 2) with 325,000 square feet (30,200 m 2) of exhibition and public space and houses over 1,000 employees.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-RC-5)

The museum's collections contain over 148 million specimens[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-CollectionsNMNH-1) of [plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant "Plant"), [animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal "Animal"), [fossils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil "Fossil"), [minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineral "Mineral"), [rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_(geology) "Rock (geology)"), [meteorites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorite "Meteorite"), human remains, and human [cultural artifacts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_artifact "Cultural artifact"), the largest natural history collection in the world.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-ABC_Interview-6) It is also home to about 185 professional natural history [scientists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientist "Scientist")—the largest group of scientists dedicated to the study of natural and cultural history in the world.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### 1846–1911

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1846–1911")]

The United States National Museum was founded in 1846 as part of the Smithsonian Institution. The museum was initially housed in the [Smithsonian Institution Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution_Building "Smithsonian Institution Building"), which is better known today as the Smithsonian Castle. A formal exhibit hall opened in 1858.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-7) The growing collection led to the construction of a new building, the National Museum Building (known today as the [Arts and Industries Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_and_Industries_Building "Arts and Industries Building")). Covering a then-enormous 2.25 acres (9,100 m 2), it was built in just 15 months at a cost of $310,000 (equivalent to $10,342,241 in 2025). It opened in March 1881.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-8)

Congress authorized construction of a new building on June 28, 1902.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-New-10) On January 29, 1903, a special committee composed of members of Congress and representatives from the Smithsonian's board of regents published a report asking Congress to fund a much larger structure than originally planned.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-New-10) The regents began considering sites for the new building in March, and by April 12 settled on a site on the north side of [B Street NW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Avenue "Constitution Avenue") between 9th and 12th Streets.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-NewPlans-12) The D.C. architectural firm of [Hornblower & Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hornblower_&_Marshall "Hornblower & Marshall") was chosen to design the structure.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-NewPlans-12) Testing of the soil for the foundations was set for July 1903, with construction expected to take three years.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-13)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Smithsonian_Natural_History_Museum_circa_1926.jpg/250px-Smithsonian_Natural_History_Museum_circa_1926.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Smithsonian_Natural_History_Museum_circa_1926.jpg)

[Ford Model T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Model_T "Ford Model T") parked in front of the National Museum in 1926

The Natural History Building (as the National Museum of Natural History was originally known) opened its doors to the public on March 17, 1910, in order to provide the Smithsonian Institution with more space for collections and research.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-14) The building was not fully completed until June 1911.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-15) The structure cost $3.5 million (equivalent to about $121 million today).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-16) The [Neoclassical style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") building was the first structure constructed on the north side of the National Mall as part of the 1901 [McMillan Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMillan_Commission "McMillan Commission") plan. In addition to the Smithsonian's natural history collection, it also housed the American history, art, and cultural collections.

### 1981–2003

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1981–2003")]

Between 1981 and 2003, the National Museum of Natural History had 11 permanent and acting directors.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-TrescottTaps-17) The directors included: [Richard S. Fiske](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Fiske "Richard S. Fiske") (1980–1985); James C. Tyler (acting, 1985 and 1988); and [Robert S. Hoffmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_S._Hoffmann "Robert S. Hoffmann") (1985–1988).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-directorsto1996-18)

[Frank Talbot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Talbot "Frank Talbot"), [ichthyologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ichthyologist "Ichthyologist") and former director of the [Australian Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Museum "Australian Museum") and [California Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Academy_of_Sciences "California Academy of Sciences"), served as director from 1989 until 1994. He was the first (and as of 2024 the only) Australian to ever be appointed to this role.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-amobit-20)

Two acting directors (Donald J. Ortner, 1994–1996, and David L. Pawson in 1996) served[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-directorsto1996-18) before Robert W. Fri was named the museum's director in 1996.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-21) One of the largest donations in Smithsonian history was made during Fri's tenure. [Kenneth E. Behring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_E._Behring "Kenneth E. Behring") donated $20 million in 1997 to modernize the museum. Fri resigned in 2001 after disagreeing with Smithsonian leadership over the reorganization of the museum's scientific research programs.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-OlsonLead-22)

[J. Dennis O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Dennis_O'Connor "J. Dennis O'Connor"), provost of the Smithsonian Institution (where he oversaw all science and research programs) was named acting director of the museum on July 25, 2001.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-23) Eight months later, O'Conner resigned to become the vice president of research and dean of the graduate school at the [University of Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland "University of Maryland").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-24)[Douglas Erwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Erwin "Douglas Erwin"), a paleontologist at the National Museum of Natural History, was appointed interim director in June 2002.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-25)
