[Video 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/18/FossiLab_video.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

A FossiLab volunteer uses lab equipment to sift through collected sediments for bone particles at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History.

The Hall of Dinosaurs has fossilized skeletons and cast models, including a _[Tyrannosaurus rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus\_rex "Tyrannosaurus rex")_ cast facing a _[Triceratops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triceratops "Triceratops")_ cast. This _Triceratops_ exhibit shows the first accurate dinosaur skeleton in virtual motion, achieved through the use of scanning and digital technology."[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-67) The collection consists of 46 "complete and important specimens" of dinosaurs.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-68)

In May 2012, billionaire David H. Koch donated $35 million toward the cost of a $45 million upgrade to the 30-year-old, 25,000 square feet (2,300 m 2) dinosaur hall. The hall closed in April 2014 and reopened in June 2019.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-69)

In June 2013, the Smithsonian obtained a 50-year lease on a _T. rex_ fossil skeleton owned by the [United States Army Corps of Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Corps_of_Engineers "United States Army Corps of Engineers"). It is the first _T. rex_ skeleton to be displayed at the museum, which until now has only had the cast of a skull. The specimen, known as the ["Wankel" or "Devil" rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specimens_of_Tyrannosaurus#%22Wankel_Rex%22:_MOR_555 "Specimens of Tyrannosaurus"),[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-70) was found on Corps-owned land in the [Charles M. Russell National Wildlife Refuge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_M._Russell_National_Wildlife_Refuge "Charles M. Russell National Wildlife Refuge") in [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana") in 1988. It has since been on display at the [Museum of the Rockies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_the_Rockies "Museum of the Rockies") in [Bozeman, Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bozeman,_Montana "Bozeman, Montana") (which helped excavate the fossil).[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-duLac-71) The "Wankel rex" (whose skeleton is 85 percent complete)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-Schontzler-72) was to be unveiled at the Museum of Natural History on National Fossil Day, October 16, 2013, and was supposed to be on display until the dinosaur hall exhibit closed for renovation in the spring of 2014. The 35-foot (11 m) long skeleton is the centerpiece of the dinosaur hall since it re-opened in 2019.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-duLac-71) The Museum of the Rockies (which did not own the skeleton but was the repository for it) has about a dozen _T. rex_ specimens, including one which is eighty percent complete. Only about six museums in the United States have a _T. rex_ skeleton. The Museum of the Rockies is a Smithsonian affiliate museum, and had long promised to find a _T. rex_ for the Smithsonian to display.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-Schontzler-72)

Due to the [2013 federal government shutdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_federal_government_shutdown_of_2013 "United States federal government shutdown of 2013"), the fossil did not arrive in Washington, D.C. Smithsonian officials said it remained in storage in Montana, and would not arrive at the Smithsonian until late spring 2014. Packed up in 16 crates, the _T. rex_, named "Nation's T. rex" by the Smithsonian, traveled from the Museum of the Rockies and arrived at the National Museum of Natural History on April 15, 2014.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-73) The _T. rex_ was displayed in the Rex Room, while specialists performed a conservation assessment and the Smithsonian Digitization Program scanned each bone, to create a 3-D model for research.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-74) The Nation's T. rex is the centerpiece of the new fossil hall, which opened in 2019.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-75)

### Hall of Mammals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Hall of Mammals")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Hall_of_Mammals_at_the_Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History.jpg/250px-Hall_of_Mammals_at_the_Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hall_of_Mammals_at_the_Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History.jpg)

View of the Hall of Mammals from above

The Behring Hall of Mammals was designed by Reich + Petch. The mammal specimens are presented as works of modern art within minimal environmentals. Visitors discover mammal's evolutionary adaptions to hugely diverse contexts.

The museum has the largest collection of [vertebrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebrate "Vertebrate") specimens in the world, nearly twice the size of the next largest mammal collections, including historically important collections from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-76) Its collection was initiated by [C. Hart Merriam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Hart_Merriam "C. Hart Merriam") and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (later the [Department of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_the_Interior "Department of the Interior")), which expanded it in the 1890s-1930s.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-77)

### Insect Zoo

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Insect Zoo")]

The **O. Orkin Insect Zoo** features live [insects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insects "Insects") and exhibits about insects and [entomologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entomologists "Entomologists"). Different habitats have been created to show the type of insects that live in different environments and how they have adapted to a [freshwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freshwater "Freshwater")[pond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pond "Pond"), house, [mangrove swamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangrove_swamp "Mangrove swamp"), [desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert "Desert"), and [rain forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_forest "Rain forest"). The zoo is sponsored by [Orkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkin "Orkin"), a pest control company.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-78)

### Ocean Hall

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Ocean Hall")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Ocean_Hall_Smithsonian_Museum_of_Natural_History.jpg/250px-Ocean_Hall_Smithsonian_Museum_of_Natural_History.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ocean_Hall_Smithsonian_Museum_of_Natural_History.jpg)

Ocean Hall

The Sant Ocean Hall opened on September 27, 2008, and is the largest renovation of the museum since it opened in 1910. The hall includes 674 marine specimens and models drawn from the over 80 million specimens in the museum's total collection, the largest in the world. The hall is named for the Roger Sant family, who donated $15 million to endow the new hall and other related programs.

The collection includes: a [North Atlantic right whale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_right_whale "North Atlantic right whale"), a giant [Lion's mane jellyfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion's_mane_jellyfish "Lion's mane jellyfish") model, a 1,500-US-gallon (5,700 L) aquarium containing live [marine fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_marine_aquarium_fish_species "List of marine aquarium fish species") and corals, one female [giant squid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_squid "Giant squid") displayed in the center of the hall and a male displayed off to the side, an adult [coelenterate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coelenterata "Coelenterata"), and a _[Basilosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilosaurus "Basilosaurus")_.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-79)

The museum also provides the [Smithsonian Ocean Portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Ocean_Portal "Smithsonian Ocean Portal"), a complementary web site that provides regularly updated, original content from the museum's research, collections, and Sant Ocean Hall as well as content provided by more than 20 collaborating organizations, including Archive, Census of Marine Life, Consortium for Ocean Leadership, Encyclopedia of Life, INDUCT, Monterey Bay Aquarium, Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, National Geographic, NOAA, New England Aquarium, [Ocean Conservancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_Conservancy "Ocean Conservancy"), Oceania, Pew Charitable Trusts, Sea Web, Save Our Seas, Scrips Institution of Oceanography, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, World Heritage Marine Programmer.

### African Voices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: African Voices")]

This exhibit and associated website "examines the diversity, dynamism, and global influence of Africa's peoples and cultures over time in the realms of family, work, community, and the natural environment."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-Current-80)

### Butterflies + Plants: Partners In Evolution

This exhibit displays a "variety of vertebrate [skeletons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeletons "Skeletons") grouped by their evolutionary relationships."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-Current-80)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Hall_of_Osteology_NMNH.jpg/250px-Hall_of_Osteology_NMNH.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hall_of_Osteology_NMNH.jpg)

### Q?rius

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Q?rius")]

Opened since 2013, this exhibit is the museum's interactive and educational area. Using microscopes and touch screens, the area hosts various interactive activities and contains a "collection zone" that houses over 6000 different specimens and artifacts visitors are able personally handle. The area also hosts various events such as allowing visitors to meet and discuss with Smithsonian scientists and hosting school groups.

### Former exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Former exhibits")]

#### Western Cultures Hall

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Western Cultures Hall")]

"This hall explores some examples from various cultures in the western world including northern Iraq, ancient Egypt, Greece and [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") and the recent discovery of the [Iceman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%96tzi_the_Iceman "Ötzi the Iceman"), a [Copper Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_Age "Copper Age")[mummy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mummy "Mummy") found in an Italian [glacier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier "Glacier")."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-Current-80) This exhibit was closed on September 26, 2010.

#### Korea Gallery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Korea Gallery")]

The Korea Gallery was a special showcase to celebrate Korean traditions and examine its unique influence and complex role in the world today.

The exhibit expressed the continuity of the past by highlighting enduring features of Korean culture over 2,600 years.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-:2-81) The exhibit used the Smithsonian ceramics collection as well as a rich selection of photographs, ritual objects and traditional Korean carpentry to communicate and connect to both the local Korean community and an international audience. Traditional art forms, such as ceramics and calligraphy, along with mythological figures, language, large feature photographs and illustrations spoke to a range of shared historical memories which connected Koreans at home and abroad.

Personal stories of modern Koreans, as told in their own voices, provide a context to discuss some of the many issues that face the divided country today. Korea's incredible transformation from 'The Hermit Kingdom' to a world power is traced through its impact on the arts, the economy and popular culture.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-:2-81) The exhibit was designed by Reich + Petch. This exhibit closed in 2017.

#### Reptiles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Reptiles")]

Reptiles on view include a preserved [King cobra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_cobra "King cobra"), [Reticulated python](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reticulated_python "Reticulated python"), and boa constrictors from the Malayan and Amazonian jungles; sea turtles; crocodiles; and lizards."[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-82) This exhibit closed in 2011.

### Baird Auditorium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Baird Auditorium")]

[![Image 22: Baird Auditorium photo take from rear of auditorium](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Baird_Auditorium%2C_SIA_2002-12145%2C_No_Rights_Restrictions.jpg/250px-Baird_Auditorium%2C_SIA_2002-12145%2C_No_Rights_Restrictions.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baird_Auditorium,_SIA_2002-12145,_No_Rights_Restrictions.jpg)

Baird Auditorium, circa 1911. Smithsonian Institution Archives Record Unit 95, Box 33, Folder: 27; Record Unit 79, Box 9, Folder: 1

Beneath the building's rotunda is the Baird Auditorium, named for the second [Secretary of the Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_the_Smithsonian "Secretary of the Smithsonian")[Spencer Fullerton Baird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Fullerton_Baird "Spencer Fullerton Baird"). The Baird Auditorium was completed in 1909, designed and built by the R. Guastavino Company under the direction of [Rafael Guastavino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Guastavino "Rafael Guastavino"), Jr. using [Catalan vault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_vault "Catalan vault") tile ceiling.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-85) The [American Institute of Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Architects "American Institute of Architects") calls the Baird Auditorium the museum's "greatest interior space."[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-86) According to architectural scholar Dr. [John Ochsendorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ochsendorf "John Ochsendorf"), the Baird Auditorium's "daring geometry" in tile construction by the [Guastavino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guastavino_tile "Guastavino tile") company "spans 90 feet (27 meters) with a remarkable shallow dome in acoustical tile, and could only have been built by a company with decades of experience in tile vaulting."[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-:1-87)

#### Baird Auditorium Events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_Natural_History&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Baird Auditorium Events")]

The Baird Auditorium has a long history of performances and events. The Baird was the location of the astronomical '[Great Debate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Debate_(astronomy) "Great Debate (astronomy)"),' also called the '[Shapley–Curtis Debate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Debate_(astronomy) "Great Debate (astronomy)"),' on April 26, 1920 on the topics of [spiral nebulae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiral_nebulae "Spiral nebulae") and the size of the universe. [Merle Travis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Travis "Merle Travis") gave a country guitar music concert in the Baird Auditorium on October 23, 1976.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-88) In early February 1977, [Muddy Waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muddy_Waters "Muddy Waters") performed in the Baird as part of the Smithsonian Institution's blues series presented by the Division of Performing Arts.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History#cite_note-89)

The **National Museum of American History: Kenneth E. Behring Center** is a historical museum in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") It collects, preserves, and displays the heritage of the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") in the areas of social, political, cultural, scientific, and military history. Among the items on display is the original [Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star-Spangled_Banner_(flag) "Star-Spangled Banner (flag)"). The [museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum "Museum") is part of the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution") and located on the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall") at [14th Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/14th_Street_(Washington,_D.C.) "14th Street (Washington, D.C.)") and [Constitution Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Avenue "Constitution Avenue") NW in Washington, D.C.

In 2023, the museum received 2.1 million visitors, ranking the [eighth-most visited museum in the U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most-visited_museums_in_the_United_States "List of most-visited museums in the United States")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-ReferenceA-1)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The museum opened in 1964 as the **Museum of History and Technology**. It was one of the last structures designed by the renowned architectural firm [McKim Mead & White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKim_Mead_&_White "McKim Mead & White"). In 1980, the museum was renamed the **National Museum of American History** to represent its mission of the collection, care, study, and interpretation of objects that reflect the experience of the American people.

The museum site had previously held two [temporary war buildings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temporary_buildings_of_the_National_Mall "Temporary buildings of the National Mall") constructed in 1942.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-map2-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-3)

In 1973, representatives of the [Committee to Re-elect the President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Committee_to_Re-elect_the_President "Committee to Re-elect the President") forced the museum to temporarily close the Right to Vote exhibit in advance of [Richard Nixon's second inauguration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Richard_Nixon "Second inauguration of Richard Nixon"). The exhibit had been designed by historian [Edith Mayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edith_Mayo "Edith Mayo").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-4)

In May 2012, [John Gray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gray_(museum_administrator) "John Gray (museum administrator)") became the new director.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-boehm-5) He retired from the post in May 2018 and was succeeded by Anthea M. Hartig who was previously chief executive of the California Historical Society.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-post-6)

### Renovations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Renovations")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/National_Museum_of_American_History_-_2026_%2855256384290%29.jpg/250px-National_Museum_of_American_History_-_2026_%2855256384290%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:National_Museum_of_American_History_-_2026_(55256384290).jpg)

The south facade of the museum

The museum underwent an $85 million renovation from September 5, 2006, to November 21, 2008,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-Kopper-7) during which time it was closed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-NMAH-8)[Skidmore, Owings and Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_and_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings and Merrill") provided the architecture and interior design services for the renovation, led by [Gary Haney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Haney "Gary Haney").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-9) Major changes made during the renovation include:

*   A new, five-story sky-lit atrium, which is surrounded by displays of artifacts that showcase the breadth of the museum's collection.
*   A new, grand staircase that links the museum's first and second floors.
*   A new welcome center, and the addition of six landmark objects to orient visitors.
*   New galleries, such as the Jerome and Dorothy Lemelson Hall of Invention.
*   An environmentally controlled chamber to protect the original [Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Spangled_Banner_Flag "Star Spangled Banner Flag") flag.

In 2012, the museum began a $37 million renovation of the west wing to add new exhibition spaces, public plazas and an education center.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-10) The renovation will also include panoramic windows overlooking the National Mall on all three floors and new interactive features to the exhibits.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-11) The first floor of the west wing reopened on July 1, 2015, with the second and third floors of the west wing reopening in 2016 and 2017, respectively.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-12)

## Layout

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Layout")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Nat._Museum_of_American_History%2C_Washington%2C_D.C._IMG_4758.JPG/250px-Nat._Museum_of_American_History%2C_Washington%2C_D.C._IMG_4758.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nat._Museum_of_American_History,_Washington,_D.C._IMG_4758.JPG)

North facade entrance of the museum

Each wing of the museum's three exhibition floors is anchored by a landmark object to highlight the theme of that wing. These include the [_John Bull_ locomotive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bull_(locomotive) "John Bull (locomotive)"), [the Greensboro, North Carolina lunch counter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensboro_sit-ins "Greensboro sit-ins"), and a one of a kind draft wheel. Landmarks from pre-existing exhibits include the 1865 Vassar Telescope, a [George Washington Statue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_(Greenough) "George Washington (Greenough)"), a [Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Red_Cross "American Red Cross") ambulance, and a car from [Disneyland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disneyland "Disneyland")'s [Dumbo Flying Elephant ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumbo_the_Flying_Elephant_(ride) "Dumbo the Flying Elephant (ride)").

Artifact walls, 275 feet (84 m) of glass-fronted cases, line the first and second floor center core. The artifact walls are organized around themes including arts; popular culture; business, work and economy; home and family; community; land and natural resources; peopling America; politics and reform; science; medicine; technology; and the United States' role in the world.

### Building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Building")]

#### Lower level

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Lower level")]

The lower level of the museum displays _Taking America to Lunch_, which celebrates the history of American lunch boxes, many decorated with pop culture. The museum's food court, the Stars and Stripes Café, and ride simulators are also located here.

#### First floor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: First floor")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/John_Bull_NMAH_side.jpg/250px-John_Bull_NMAH_side.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Bull_NMAH_side.jpg)

_[John Bull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John\_Bull\_(locomotive) "John Bull (locomotive)")_, an 1831 locomotive displayed in _America on the Move_, a first-floor exhibit

The first floor's East Wing (called 1 East) has exhibits that feature transportation and technology; they include _America on the Move_ and _Lighting a Revolution._ The [_John Bull_ locomotive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bull_(locomotive) "John Bull (locomotive)") is the signature artifact. Exhibits within _America on the Move_ include [Southern Railway locomotive no. 1401](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Railway_1401 "Southern Railway 1401"), [Santa Cruz Railroad no. 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Railroad_no._3 "Santa Cruz Railroad no. 3"), and a [Chicago "L"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22 "Chicago \"L\"") elevated station diorama featuring a [CTA 6000-series railcar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6000-series_(CTA) "6000-series (CTA)").

The exhibits in the West Wing (1 West) address science and innovation. They include _Science in American Life featuring Robots on the Road_ and _Bon Appétit! [Julia Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia\_Child "Julia Child")'s Kitchen._ _Spark!Lab_ is a hands-on exhibit of the Lemelson Center for the Study of Invention and Innovation. The Vassar Telescope is the signature artifact.

A café and the main museum store are also located on the first floor. The first floor also contains the Constitution Avenue lobby (1 Center), as well as a space for a temporary exhibit.

#### Second floor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Second floor")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/George_Washington_Greenough_statue.jpg/250px-George_Washington_Greenough_statue.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Washington_Greenough_statue.jpg)

_[George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George\_Washington\_(Greenough) "George Washington (Greenough)")_, 1840, by [Horatio Greenough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Greenough "Horatio Greenough")

The exhibitions in 2 East, the east wing of the second floor, consider American ideals and include the Albert Small Documents Gallery featuring rotating exhibits. From November 21, 2008, through January 4, 2009, an original copy of the [Gettysburg Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gettysburg_Address "Gettysburg Address"), on loan from the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), was on display. The [Greensboro lunch counter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensboro_sit-ins "Greensboro sit-ins") is the signature artifact for this section of the museum.

Located in the center of the second floor (2 Center) is the original [Star Spangled Banner Flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Spangled_Banner_Flag "Star Spangled Banner Flag") which inspired [Francis Scott Key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Scott_Key "Francis Scott Key")'s [poem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Star-Spangled_Banner "The Star-Spangled Banner"). The newly conserved flag, the centerpiece of the renovated museum, is displayed in a climate-controlled room at the heart of the museum. An interactive display by [Potion Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potion_Design "Potion Design"), just across the room from the flag, features a full-size, digital reproduction of the flag that allows patrons to learn more about it by touching different areas on the flag.

The _[George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George\_Washington\_(Greenough) "George Washington (Greenough)")_ statue, sculpted by [Horatio Greenough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Greenough "Horatio Greenough") for exhibit in the [Rotunda of the United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Rotunda "Capitol Rotunda") and in celebration of the centennial of Washington's birth, is the signature artifact for 2 West, the west wing of the second floor of the museum.

An entire eighteenth century [colonial house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_colonial_architecture "American colonial architecture"), the [Choate-Caldwell House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choate-Caldwell_House "Choate-Caldwell House") (c.1710/1760) from [Ipswich, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ipswich,_Massachusetts "Ipswich, Massachusetts") is located on the second floor (in 2 West) as part of the "Within These Walls" exhibit.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-13)

The second floor also houses the museum's new welcome center and a store. The second-floor lobby leads out to Madison Drive and the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall").

#### Third floor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Third floor")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/GunboatPhiladelphia.jpg/250px-GunboatPhiladelphia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GunboatPhiladelphia.jpg)

The gunboat _[Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS\_Philadelphia\_(1776) "USS Philadelphia (1776)")_

Exhibits in the east wing of the third floor, 3 East, are focused on the military history of the United States; they include _The Price of Freedom: Americans at War_ and the gunboat _[Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS\_Philadelphia\_(1776) "USS Philadelphia (1776)")_.

The center of the third floor, 3 Center, presents _The American Presidency: A Glorious Burden_, which explores the personal and public lives of the men who have held that office. It also features the popular permanent exhibit of _[First Ladies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First\_Lady\_of\_the\_United\_States "First Lady of the United States") of America_, which features their contributions and changing roles, and displays their dresses as a mark of changing times.

The third-floor west wing, 3 West, has exhibits that feature entertainment, sports, and music. These include _Thanks for the Memories: Music, Sports and Entertainment History_, the Hall of Musical Instruments, and _The Dolls' House_. A car from [Disneyland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disneyland "Disneyland")'s [Dumbo the Flying Elephant ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumbo_the_Flying_Elephant_(ride) "Dumbo the Flying Elephant (ride)"). The most recent exhibit is _Entertainment Nation_ which features objects from Judy Garland, Prince, Selena, Muhammad Ali, _Star Wars_, _Sesame Street_, _Hamilton_, and more.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-14)

On the Third floor west, the Gypsy Rose is currently featured in the new exhibit "Corazón y vida: Lowriding Culture" and will remain on display from September 2025 through October 2027.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-15) The Gypsy Rose is one of the most iconic lowriders. Featured in the opening credits of the 1970s television show Chico and the Man, as well as in the 1979 film Boulevard Nights, this car thrust lowriding into the popular imagination. Custom interiors and hand-painted roses make the car stand out while cruising the streets of Los Angeles and help set the standard for lowriders today. Other lowriders of the time drew inspiration from this car’s unique details, such as its interior candle sconce.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-16)

### Outdoor sculptures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Outdoor sculptures")]

In 1967, the 24-foot-tall (7.3 m)[abstract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_art "Abstract art")[sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculpture "Sculpture")_[Infinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinity\_(de\_Rivera) "Infinity (de Rivera)")_ was dedicated at the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall") entrance.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-17) Designed by [José de Rivera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_de_Rivera "Jose de Rivera") and created by [Roy Gussow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Gussow "Roy Gussow"), it was one of the first abstract sculptures displayed at a major [public building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_building "Public building") in Washington D.C. The sculpture is a 16-foot-long (4.9 m), polished stainless steel ribbon on top of a granite tower.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-nytimes-18)

[Alexander Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Calder "Alexander Calder")'s sculpture _[Gwenfritz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwenfritz "Gwenfritz")_ was installed in a fountain on the west side. The steel abstract [stabile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Calder "Alexander Calder") was dedicated to the museum on June 2, 1969. In 1984, the museum moved the work to a site closer to Constitution Avenue until July 2013, when conservators removed it for restoration. The sculpture returned to its original site in November 2014, and sits in the midst of a re-created reflecting pool.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-19) Calder's original plan for the sculpture envisioned it surrounded by water jets, but architects and engineers of the site determined that the fountain would be challenging to maintain and the water spray would hasten deterioration of the metal.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-20)

### Archives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Archives")]

In support of the museum's mission, the Archives Center identifies, acquires, and preserves significant archival records in many media and formats to document America's history and its diverse cultures. Center staff arrange, describe, preserve, and make collections accessible in support of scholarship, exhibitions, publications, and education.

The Archives Center occupies over 12,000 feet (3,700 m) of shelving in the National Museum of American History building. Subject strengths include the history of the radio, television, the telegraph, computing, and other aspects of the history of technology with a special interest in the history of invention; advertising, marketing, and entrepreneurship; commercial visual ephemera (postcards, greeting cards); American music (sheet music, jazz) and musical instruments. These, and a wide range of other subjects, are documented in business records, personal papers, and extensive holdings of motion picture film, video and sound recordings, historical photographs, and oral histories.

### Jerome and Dorothy Lemelson Center for the Study of Invention and Innovation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Jerome and Dorothy Lemelson Center for the Study of Invention and Innovation")]

The Lemelson Center, an initiative of the [Lemelson Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemelson_Foundation "Lemelson Foundation"), produces educational programs, popular and academic publications, exhibitions, podcasts and symposia about invention. The mission of the Lemelson Center is to document, interpret and disseminate information about invention and innovation, encourage creativity in young people, and foster an appreciation for the central role of innovation in the history of the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). The Center frequently provides a multi-year focus on some aspect of how invention has influenced American society, such as its 2002 "Invention and the Environment" theme. Programs include an annual symposium, presentations and guest speakers, and often the publication of a book highlighting a particular topic.

The Center provides free curricular material to classrooms throughout the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), organizes traveling museum exhibitions (such as _Invention at Play_), and provides research opportunities. It obtains archival collections related to invention for the museum's Archives Center. Such collections consist of the papers and materials that document the work of past and current American inventors.

## Past exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Past exhibits")]

*   _Slavery at Jefferson's Monticello: Paradox of Liberty_, January 27 – October 14, 2012, Smithsonian Institution, a landmark exhibit, the first ever on the Mall to explore a president's relation to slavery; it focused on six major slave families at [Monticello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monticello "Monticello").
*   _[24 Hours in Cyberspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24\_Hours\_in\_Cyberspace "24 Hours in Cyberspace")_ – opened on January 23, 1997, this exhibit celebrated "the largest one-day online event" (February 8, 1996) up to that date, which took place on the then-active website, _cyber24.com_ (it is online at a [mirror website](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_website "Mirror website") maintained by [Georgia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Tech "Georgia Tech")).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-27)_24 Hours in Cyberspace_ was headed by photographer [Rick Smolan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Smolan "Rick Smolan").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-28) The exhibit featured 70 photos from the project.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-29)
*   _Treasures of American History_, temporary display at the [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum"), closed in April 2008.
*   _A Nation of Nations_ was the Smithsonian's [Bicentennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bicentennial "American Bicentennial") salute to the American immigrant experience; it included many iconic rooms and examples of immigrants' contribution to the United States.

The **National Museum of American History: Kenneth E. Behring Center** is a historical museum in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") It collects, preserves, and displays the heritage of the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") in the areas of social, political, cultural, scientific, and military history. Among the items on display is the original [Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star-Spangled_Banner_(flag) "Star-Spangled Banner (flag)"). The [museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum "Museum") is part of the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution") and located on the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall") at [14th Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/14th_Street_(Washington,_D.C.) "14th Street (Washington, D.C.)") and [Constitution Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Avenue "Constitution Avenue") NW in Washington, D.C.

In 2023, the museum received 2.1 million visitors, ranking the [eighth-most visited museum in the U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most-visited_museums_in_the_United_States "List of most-visited museums in the United States")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-ReferenceA-1)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The museum opened in 1964 as the **Museum of History and Technology**. It was one of the last structures designed by the renowned architectural firm [McKim Mead & White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKim_Mead_&_White "McKim Mead & White"). In 1980, the museum was renamed the **National Museum of American History** to represent its mission of the collection, care, study, and interpretation of objects that reflect the experience of the American people.

The museum site had previously held two [temporary war buildings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temporary_buildings_of_the_National_Mall "Temporary buildings of the National Mall") constructed in 1942.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-map2-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-3)

In 1973, representatives of the [Committee to Re-elect the President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Committee_to_Re-elect_the_President "Committee to Re-elect the President") forced the museum to temporarily close the Right to Vote exhibit in advance of [Richard Nixon's second inauguration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Richard_Nixon "Second inauguration of Richard Nixon"). The exhibit had been designed by historian [Edith Mayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edith_Mayo "Edith Mayo").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-4)

In May 2012, [John Gray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gray_(museum_administrator) "John Gray (museum administrator)") became the new director.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-boehm-5) He retired from the post in May 2018 and was succeeded by Anthea M. Hartig who was previously chief executive of the California Historical Society.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-post-6)

### Renovations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Renovations")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/National_Museum_of_American_History_-_2026_%2855256384290%29.jpg/250px-National_Museum_of_American_History_-_2026_%2855256384290%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:National_Museum_of_American_History_-_2026_(55256384290).jpg)

The south facade of the museum

The museum underwent an $85 million renovation from September 5, 2006, to November 21, 2008,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-Kopper-7) during which time it was closed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-NMAH-8)[Skidmore, Owings and Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_and_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings and Merrill") provided the architecture and interior design services for the renovation, led by [Gary Haney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Haney "Gary Haney").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-9) Major changes made during the renovation include:

*   A new, five-story sky-lit atrium, which is surrounded by displays of artifacts that showcase the breadth of the museum's collection.
*   A new, grand staircase that links the museum's first and second floors.
*   A new welcome center, and the addition of six landmark objects to orient visitors.
*   New galleries, such as the Jerome and Dorothy Lemelson Hall of Invention.
*   An environmentally controlled chamber to protect the original [Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Spangled_Banner_Flag "Star Spangled Banner Flag") flag.

In 2012, the museum began a $37 million renovation of the west wing to add new exhibition spaces, public plazas and an education center.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-10) The renovation will also include panoramic windows overlooking the National Mall on all three floors and new interactive features to the exhibits.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-11) The first floor of the west wing reopened on July 1, 2015, with the second and third floors of the west wing reopening in 2016 and 2017, respectively.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-12)

## Layout

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Layout")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Nat._Museum_of_American_History%2C_Washington%2C_D.C._IMG_4758.JPG/250px-Nat._Museum_of_American_History%2C_Washington%2C_D.C._IMG_4758.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nat._Museum_of_American_History,_Washington,_D.C._IMG_4758.JPG)

North facade entrance of the museum

Each wing of the museum's three exhibition floors is anchored by a landmark object to highlight the theme of that wing. These include the [_John Bull_ locomotive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bull_(locomotive) "John Bull (locomotive)"), [the Greensboro, North Carolina lunch counter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensboro_sit-ins "Greensboro sit-ins"), and a one of a kind draft wheel. Landmarks from pre-existing exhibits include the 1865 Vassar Telescope, a [George Washington Statue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_(Greenough) "George Washington (Greenough)"), a [Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Red_Cross "American Red Cross") ambulance, and a car from [Disneyland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disneyland "Disneyland")'s [Dumbo Flying Elephant ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumbo_the_Flying_Elephant_(ride) "Dumbo the Flying Elephant (ride)").

Artifact walls, 275 feet (84 m) of glass-fronted cases, line the first and second floor center core. The artifact walls are organized around themes including arts; popular culture; business, work and economy; home and family; community; land and natural resources; peopling America; politics and reform; science; medicine; technology; and the United States' role in the world.

### Building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Building")]

#### Lower level

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Lower level")]

The lower level of the museum displays _Taking America to Lunch_, which celebrates the history of American lunch boxes, many decorated with pop culture. The museum's food court, the Stars and Stripes Café, and ride simulators are also located here.

#### First floor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: First floor")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/John_Bull_NMAH_side.jpg/250px-John_Bull_NMAH_side.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Bull_NMAH_side.jpg)

_[John Bull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John\_Bull\_(locomotive) "John Bull (locomotive)")_, an 1831 locomotive displayed in _America on the Move_, a first-floor exhibit

The first floor's East Wing (called 1 East) has exhibits that feature transportation and technology; they include _America on the Move_ and _Lighting a Revolution._ The [_John Bull_ locomotive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bull_(locomotive) "John Bull (locomotive)") is the signature artifact. Exhibits within _America on the Move_ include [Southern Railway locomotive no. 1401](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Railway_1401 "Southern Railway 1401"), [Santa Cruz Railroad no. 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Railroad_no._3 "Santa Cruz Railroad no. 3"), and a [Chicago "L"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22 "Chicago \"L\"") elevated station diorama featuring a [CTA 6000-series railcar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6000-series_(CTA) "6000-series (CTA)").

The exhibits in the West Wing (1 West) address science and innovation. They include _Science in American Life featuring Robots on the Road_ and _Bon Appétit! [Julia Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia\_Child "Julia Child")'s Kitchen._ _Spark!Lab_ is a hands-on exhibit of the Lemelson Center for the Study of Invention and Innovation. The Vassar Telescope is the signature artifact.

A café and the main museum store are also located on the first floor. The first floor also contains the Constitution Avenue lobby (1 Center), as well as a space for a temporary exhibit.

#### Second floor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Second floor")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/George_Washington_Greenough_statue.jpg/250px-George_Washington_Greenough_statue.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Washington_Greenough_statue.jpg)

_[George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George\_Washington\_(Greenough) "George Washington (Greenough)")_, 1840, by [Horatio Greenough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Greenough "Horatio Greenough")

The exhibitions in 2 East, the east wing of the second floor, consider American ideals and include the Albert Small Documents Gallery featuring rotating exhibits. From November 21, 2008, through January 4, 2009, an original copy of the [Gettysburg Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gettysburg_Address "Gettysburg Address"), on loan from the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), was on display. The [Greensboro lunch counter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensboro_sit-ins "Greensboro sit-ins") is the signature artifact for this section of the museum.

Located in the center of the second floor (2 Center) is the original [Star Spangled Banner Flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Spangled_Banner_Flag "Star Spangled Banner Flag") which inspired [Francis Scott Key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Scott_Key "Francis Scott Key")'s [poem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Star-Spangled_Banner "The Star-Spangled Banner"). The newly conserved flag, the centerpiece of the renovated museum, is displayed in a climate-controlled room at the heart of the museum. An interactive display by [Potion Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potion_Design "Potion Design"), just across the room from the flag, features a full-size, digital reproduction of the flag that allows patrons to learn more about it by touching different areas on the flag.

The _[George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George\_Washington\_(Greenough) "George Washington (Greenough)")_ statue, sculpted by [Horatio Greenough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Greenough "Horatio Greenough") for exhibit in the [Rotunda of the United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Rotunda "Capitol Rotunda") and in celebration of the centennial of Washington's birth, is the signature artifact for 2 West, the west wing of the second floor of the museum.

An entire eighteenth century [colonial house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_colonial_architecture "American colonial architecture"), the [Choate-Caldwell House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choate-Caldwell_House "Choate-Caldwell House") (c.1710/1760) from [Ipswich, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ipswich,_Massachusetts "Ipswich, Massachusetts") is located on the second floor (in 2 West) as part of the "Within These Walls" exhibit.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-13)

The second floor also houses the museum's new welcome center and a store. The second-floor lobby leads out to Madison Drive and the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall").

#### Third floor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Third floor")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/GunboatPhiladelphia.jpg/250px-GunboatPhiladelphia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GunboatPhiladelphia.jpg)

The gunboat _[Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS\_Philadelphia\_(1776) "USS Philadelphia (1776)")_

Exhibits in the east wing of the third floor, 3 East, are focused on the military history of the United States; they include _The Price of Freedom: Americans at War_ and the gunboat _[Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS\_Philadelphia\_(1776) "USS Philadelphia (1776)")_.

The center of the third floor, 3 Center, presents _The American Presidency: A Glorious Burden_, which explores the personal and public lives of the men who have held that office. It also features the popular permanent exhibit of _[First Ladies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First\_Lady\_of\_the\_United\_States "First Lady of the United States") of America_, which features their contributions and changing roles, and displays their dresses as a mark of changing times.

The third-floor west wing, 3 West, has exhibits that feature entertainment, sports, and music. These include _Thanks for the Memories: Music, Sports and Entertainment History_, the Hall of Musical Instruments, and _The Dolls' House_. A car from [Disneyland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disneyland "Disneyland")'s [Dumbo the Flying Elephant ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumbo_the_Flying_Elephant_(ride) "Dumbo the Flying Elephant (ride)"). The most recent exhibit is _Entertainment Nation_ which features objects from Judy Garland, Prince, Selena, Muhammad Ali, _Star Wars_, _Sesame Street_, _Hamilton_, and more.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-14)

On the Third floor west, the Gypsy Rose is currently featured in the new exhibit "Corazón y vida: Lowriding Culture" and will remain on display from September 2025 through October 2027.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-15) The Gypsy Rose is one of the most iconic lowriders. Featured in the opening credits of the 1970s television show Chico and the Man, as well as in the 1979 film Boulevard Nights, this car thrust lowriding into the popular imagination. Custom interiors and hand-painted roses make the car stand out while cruising the streets of Los Angeles and help set the standard for lowriders today. Other lowriders of the time drew inspiration from this car’s unique details, such as its interior candle sconce.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-16)

### Outdoor sculptures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Outdoor sculptures")]

In 1967, the 24-foot-tall (7.3 m)[abstract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_art "Abstract art")[sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculpture "Sculpture")_[Infinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinity\_(de\_Rivera) "Infinity (de Rivera)")_ was dedicated at the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall") entrance.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-17) Designed by [José de Rivera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_de_Rivera "Jose de Rivera") and created by [Roy Gussow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Gussow "Roy Gussow"), it was one of the first abstract sculptures displayed at a major [public building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_building "Public building") in Washington D.C. The sculpture is a 16-foot-long (4.9 m), polished stainless steel ribbon on top of a granite tower.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-nytimes-18)

[Alexander Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Calder "Alexander Calder")'s sculpture _[Gwenfritz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwenfritz "Gwenfritz")_ was installed in a fountain on the west side. The steel abstract [stabile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Calder "Alexander Calder") was dedicated to the museum on June 2, 1969. In 1984, the museum moved the work to a site closer to Constitution Avenue until July 2013, when conservators removed it for restoration. The sculpture returned to its original site in November 2014, and sits in the midst of a re-created reflecting pool.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-19) Calder's original plan for the sculpture envisioned it surrounded by water jets, but architects and engineers of the site determined that the fountain would be challenging to maintain and the water spray would hasten deterioration of the metal.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-20)

### Archives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Archives")]

In support of the museum's mission, the Archives Center identifies, acquires, and preserves significant archival records in many media and formats to document America's history and its diverse cultures. Center staff arrange, describe, preserve, and make collections accessible in support of scholarship, exhibitions, publications, and education.

The Archives Center occupies over 12,000 feet (3,700 m) of shelving in the National Museum of American History building. Subject strengths include the history of the radio, television, the telegraph, computing, and other aspects of the history of technology with a special interest in the history of invention; advertising, marketing, and entrepreneurship; commercial visual ephemera (postcards, greeting cards); American music (sheet music, jazz) and musical instruments. These, and a wide range of other subjects, are documented in business records, personal papers, and extensive holdings of motion picture film, video and sound recordings, historical photographs, and oral histories.

### Jerome and Dorothy Lemelson Center for the Study of Invention and Innovation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Jerome and Dorothy Lemelson Center for the Study of Invention and Innovation")]

The Lemelson Center, an initiative of the [Lemelson Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemelson_Foundation "Lemelson Foundation"), produces educational programs, popular and academic publications, exhibitions, podcasts and symposia about invention. The mission of the Lemelson Center is to document, interpret and disseminate information about invention and innovation, encourage creativity in young people, and foster an appreciation for the central role of innovation in the history of the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). The Center frequently provides a multi-year focus on some aspect of how invention has influenced American society, such as its 2002 "Invention and the Environment" theme. Programs include an annual symposium, presentations and guest speakers, and often the publication of a book highlighting a particular topic.

The Center provides free curricular material to classrooms throughout the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), organizes traveling museum exhibitions (such as _Invention at Play_), and provides research opportunities. It obtains archival collections related to invention for the museum's Archives Center. Such collections consist of the papers and materials that document the work of past and current American inventors.

## Past exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Museum_of_American_History&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Past exhibits")]

*   _Slavery at Jefferson's Monticello: Paradox of Liberty_, January 27 – October 14, 2012, Smithsonian Institution, a landmark exhibit, the first ever on the Mall to explore a president's relation to slavery; it focused on six major slave families at [Monticello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monticello "Monticello").
*   _[24 Hours in Cyberspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24\_Hours\_in\_Cyberspace "24 Hours in Cyberspace")_ – opened on January 23, 1997, this exhibit celebrated "the largest one-day online event" (February 8, 1996) up to that date, which took place on the then-active website, _cyber24.com_ (it is online at a [mirror website](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_website "Mirror website") maintained by [Georgia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Tech "Georgia Tech")).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-27)_24 Hours in Cyberspace_ was headed by photographer [Rick Smolan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Smolan "Rick Smolan").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-28) The exhibit featured 70 photos from the project.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History#cite_note-29)
*   _Treasures of American History_, temporary display at the [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum"), closed in April 2008.
*   _A Nation of Nations_ was the Smithsonian's [Bicentennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bicentennial "American Bicentennial") salute to the American immigrant experience; it included many iconic rooms and examples of immigrants' contribution to the United States.

This is a complete **List of National Historic Landmarks in Oregon**. The [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")[National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") (NHL) program is operated under the auspices of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), and recognizes buildings, structures, districts, objects, and similar resources [nationwide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._National_Historic_Landmarks_by_state "List of U.S. National Historic Landmarks by state") according to a list of criteria of national significance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The [state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon "Oregon") is home to 17 of these landmarks, two of which extend beyond Oregon's borders into other states, as well as one site from which NHL status was withdrawn upon its destruction.

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

Main article: [National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark")

The National Historic Landmark program is administered by the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), a branch of the U.S. [Department of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Interior "United States Department of the Interior"). The National Park Service determines which properties meet NHL criteria and makes nomination recommendations after an owner notification process.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The [Secretary of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Interior "United States Secretary of the Interior") reviews nominations and, based on a set of predetermined criteria, makes a decision on NHL designation or a determination of eligibility for designation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-Title36-2) Both public and privately owned properties are designated as NHLs. This designation provides indirect, partial protection of the historic integrity of the properties, via tax incentives, grants, monitoring of threats, and other means.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-NHLQA-1) Owners may object to the nomination of the property as an NHL; when this is the case the Secretary of the Interior can only designate a site as eligible for designation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-Title36-2)

NHLs are also included on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") (NRHP), which are historic properties that the National Park Service deems to be worthy of preservation. The primary difference between an NHL and a NRHP listing is that the NHLs are determined to have particular national significance, while other NRHP properties may be deemed significant at the local or state level.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The NHLs in Oregon comprise 0.8% of the approximately 1,900 properties and districts listed on the [NRHP in Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places_listings_in_Oregon "National Register of Historic Places listings in Oregon").

This is a complete **List of National Historic Landmarks in Oregon**. The [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")[National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") (NHL) program is operated under the auspices of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), and recognizes buildings, structures, districts, objects, and similar resources [nationwide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._National_Historic_Landmarks_by_state "List of U.S. National Historic Landmarks by state") according to a list of criteria of national significance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The [state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon "Oregon") is home to 17 of these landmarks, two of which extend beyond Oregon's borders into other states, as well as one site from which NHL status was withdrawn upon its destruction.

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

Main article: [National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark")

The National Historic Landmark program is administered by the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), a branch of the U.S. [Department of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Interior "United States Department of the Interior"). The National Park Service determines which properties meet NHL criteria and makes nomination recommendations after an owner notification process.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The [Secretary of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Interior "United States Secretary of the Interior") reviews nominations and, based on a set of predetermined criteria, makes a decision on NHL designation or a determination of eligibility for designation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-Title36-2) Both public and privately owned properties are designated as NHLs. This designation provides indirect, partial protection of the historic integrity of the properties, via tax incentives, grants, monitoring of threats, and other means.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-NHLQA-1) Owners may object to the nomination of the property as an NHL; when this is the case the Secretary of the Interior can only designate a site as eligible for designation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-Title36-2)

NHLs are also included on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") (NRHP), which are historic properties that the National Park Service deems to be worthy of preservation. The primary difference between an NHL and a NRHP listing is that the NHLs are determined to have particular national significance, while other NRHP properties may be deemed significant at the local or state level.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The NHLs in Oregon comprise 0.8% of the approximately 1,900 properties and districts listed on the [NRHP in Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places_listings_in_Oregon "National Register of Historic Places listings in Oregon").

The canned salmon industry was a cornerstone of the [Northwest's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_United_States "Northwestern United States") resource-based economy from the late 1860s until after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). Amid seasonal and declining salmon stocks, the cannery diversified into [tuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuna "Tuna") in the 1930s. Because of structural deterioration, the building was slated for demolition in 1991, and it burned in 1993.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Oregon#cite_note-12) |
